author: AdamWill
body:
When 0.2.36 landed in Fedora Rawhide recently, ostree install tests on UEFI started failing (BIOS installs are still OK). The install apparently succeeds, but the installed system [boots to the grub emergency shell](https://openqa.fedoraproject.org/tests/5173872#step/_graphical_wait_login/1).

In the install logs, we see this:
```
Could not find /boot/efi/EFI when installing "EFI/fedora/grub.cfg"
```
which looks pretty significant. Indeed if I run an install and do not reboot at the end, but go to a console and check `/mnt/sysroot/boot/efi/EFI/fedora` (`/mnt/sysroot` is where the Fedora installer mounts the installed system root) it contains no `grub.cfg`, which is very likely the issue. (It also seems odd that the failure to install this file is just logged as an info, but the bootupctl command still exits 0?)

On a hunch, I tested a [scratch build](https://koji.fedoraproject.org/koji/taskinfo?taskID=149341885) with #1126 reverted, and it [passed tests](https://openqa.stg.fedoraproject.org/tests/overview?version=46&distri=fedora&groupid=2&build=Kojitask-149341885-NOREPORT). So it looks like that PR is the cause, @Johan-Liebert1 .

I'll send an official Fedora build with the PR reverted for now, but it'd be great to get a proper fix for this. CC @cgwalters . To reproduce, just try installing from e.g. https://kojipkgs.fedoraproject.org/compose/rawhide/Fedora-Rawhide-20260821.n.0/compose/Silverblue/x86_64/iso/Fedora-Silverblue-Installer-Rawhide-20260821.n.0.x86_64.iso on a UEFI system or VM, and booting the installed system.
title: Fedora ostree installer image installs broken on UEFI with 0.2.36 due to #1126

author: Rolv-Apneseth
body:
This is related to https://github.com/coreos/fedora-coreos-tracker/issues/1623, and adds a [varlink](https://varlink.org/) interface that `fwupd` can use to tell `bootupd` to sync firmware capsule updates to other co-located ESPs for our RAID setups (redundant ESPs).

There is already a [related `fwupd` PR](https://github.com/fwupd/fwupd/pull/10851), which @hughsie built against [a copr project I created](https://copr.fedorainfracloud.org/coprs/rapneset/bootupd-varlink/). The tests included here should confirm we're working as intended though.

The way it works is it accepts a `partuuid` of the device the update was written to, and a `capsule_dir` with the relative path to the update dir on the device, and syncs those updates across co-located ESPs by mounting each in turn. On my system, I can interact with the interface like this:

```sh
sudo dnf copr enable rapneset/bootupd-varlink
sudo dnf install bootupd-0.3d32bdb --repo 'copr:copr.fedorainfracloud.org:rapneset:bootupd-varlink'
sudo systemctl start bootupd-varlink.socket
sudo varlinkctl call /run/bootupd/org.coreos.bootupd1 \
  org.coreos.bootupd1.SyncFwupdUpdates \
  '{"partuuid": "2e126947-2730-49df-af3f-012de73bccfd", "capsule_dir": "EFI/fedora/fw"}'
```

Couple notes:

- Put the `varlink` subcommand under `bootupd` since it shouldn't be user-facing
- Implemented a simple service first, but now I'm leaning mostly towards socket-activated (both currently implemented)
- Socket will need to be enabled in `fedora-coreos-config`. We'll also need to have `udisks2` for `fwupd` to work as intended.
- I haven't made any updates to the readme just yet - waiting to see if we want to make any changes to the approach here
- RAID tests are divided by architecture just like the [raid1-boot](https://github.com/coreos/fedora-coreos-config/tree/testing-devel/tests/kola/boot/raid1-boot) tests
- Since `zlink` required an async runtime, I chose `smol` as a lightweight option
title: varlink: add varlink interface for syncing fwupd capsule updates across ESPs

author: c4rt0
body:
Superseeds the TMT approach in [bootupd](https://github.com/coreos/bootupd/pull/967).

This follows the approach used for [console-login-helper-messages](https://github.com/coreos/console-login-helper-messages/pull/136), while using bootupd’s Rust packaging tooling.

* Add FMF/TMT smoke-test metadata.
* Add a minimal bootupd --version smoke test. 
* Support two TMT modes:
  * GitHub Actions builds the PR source and runs the source-built binary.
  * Packit/Testing Farm installs the RPM built from the PR source.
* Add Packit copr_build and tests jobs for Fedora Rawhide and CentOS Stream 10.
* Add cargo xtask spec to generate a spec referencing the PR-versioned .crate source and filtered vendor archive.
* Do not add gating.yaml; OSCI auto-detects TMT tests.

The original bootupd #967 workflow installed a stock distribution RPM, so it did not test PR content.  This change addresses that by having Packit build the PR RPM in Copr before Testing Farm runs the TMT smoke plan.bootupctl status and real bootloader-update behavior need an EFI-capable bootc/CoreOS-style environment. This is initial smoke testing - image-mode functional coverage can follow separately.
title: Add TMT gating tests and Packit CI

author: krolmiki2011
body:
Thanks to these changes, it will be possible to eliminate the rpm dependency from bootupd and become more distribution-independent!

KEY CHANGES:
BIOS:
In the case of BIOS, ContentMetadata is created just as it is for UEFI; for BIOS, `grub2-install --version` and the `mtime` are used.
EFI (ostree-boot):
The situation is similar for ostree-boot in BIOS mode, except it iterates through files, and the version format is: legacy-ostree-boot-{mtime}

NOTE:
The old code, before the modification, is in the {bios, efi, packagesystem}_legacy.rs

Oh, and 'grub2-install --version' need package maintainers to patch grub2 upstream version to package version

This patch was inspired by issue: #468
title: Drop RPM dependency and move system packaging concerns to external scripts

author: Johan-Liebert1
body:
state: Skip state check for GrubCC and Systemd on non-efi systems

We were relying on `cfg(efi_arch)` to check for the existence of
bootupd's statefile, but that's not correct.

Using just `cfg(efi_arch)` is insufficient, as if the binary's
built on x86, but the target system is only BIOS, then we WILL enter
the branch which will want to check the statefile in the ESP and will
encounter an error.

Also, skip statefile check if we're only installing for BIOS and we do
not have EFI component

---

tests: Add bootc install tests for BIOS and UEFI

Also check whether the final VM boots or not

Related to: #1139
title: BIOS Fix

author: ci-robbot
body:
Ref: kairos-io/kairos#4445 (option 1 from https://github.com/kairos-io/kairos/issues/4445#issuecomment-5524873972).

Reverses the `Dockerfile.tmpl` + `envsubst` render step introduced in b31792d and makes the committed `Dockerfile` itself the source of truth. Every one of the 106 cached-package versions moves into the global `ARG` block as `ARG <NAME>_VERSION=<version>`; Docker interpolates the same `${<NAME>_VERSION}` placeholders in `FROM` lines natively at build time, exactly as it already did for `FIPS`, `KERNEL_TYPE`, `BOOTLOADER` and `TARGETARCH` in this same file.

## Verification: the migration is provably a no-op

Rendering the old `Dockerfile.tmpl` through envsubst against `sources.yaml`, and expanding the new committed `Dockerfile` with the same variables, produces byte-for-byte the same file. Only the added ARG block differs:

```
$ diff old-rendered.dockerfile new-rendered.dockerfile
--- old
+++ new
@@ -24,6 +24,118 @@
 ARG GNU_MIRROR_3=https://mirror.netcologne.de/gnu

+## Cached-package versions.
+## Single source of truth for the versions this project builds against.
+## Each ${<name>_VERSION} in the FROM lines below expands to the default here.
+## sources.yaml carries the matching urls + sha256 + filename metadata, keyed by version_arg.
+## To bump a package: change the ARG default here AND update the sha256 in sources.yaml.
+ARG ACL_VERSION=2.4.0
+ARG APORTS_VERSION=3.24.1
+... (106 lines total)
+ARG ZSTD_VERSION=1.5.7
```

Every one of the 106 resolved `FROM` refs is byte-identical to what `envsubst` produced from `Dockerfile.tmpl`.

`git` detected the rename at 98% similarity (`rename Dockerfile.tmpl => Dockerfile (98%)`), which is the same signal from the other side.

## Why

- One file to edit on a version bump (the Dockerfile).
- `docker build .` off a fresh clone works with no prerequisite render step and no python / PyYAML / envsubst on the host.
- The nightly autobumper (updatecli against Dockerfile) stops silently failing on a gitignored artifact; every night since 2026-08-23 had been dying with `open Dockerfile: no such file or directory`. Same root cause as #582 (which writes bumps to `sources.yaml` instead); this can supersede it.
- Removes the render / rendered-artifact drift class of bugs by construction.

## What changed

- `Dockerfile.tmpl` -> `Dockerfile`. Added `ARG <NAME>_VERSION=<version>` for each of the 106 packages previously templated. Dropped `/Dockerfile` from `.gitignore`.
- `sources.yaml`: dropped the `version:` field from every package entry. It now carries only fetch metadata (`version_arg` / `sha256` / `urls` / `filename`) keyed by the `version_arg` the Dockerfile declares. Header comment updated to explain the new split.
- `hack/render.sh`: slimmed to the fork-PR upstream mode only. Trusted builds no longer invoke it; fork PRs rewrite `FROM ghcr.io/.../pkg` lines with checksum-verifying downloader stages, reading the pinned version from the Dockerfile ARG default (via the `version_arg` map in `sources.yaml`) instead of from `sources.yaml`'s `version` field.
- `.github/actions/render-dockerfile/action.yml`: composite becomes a fork-PR-only helper. First step exits early on trusted builds (no-op); upstream-mode steps only run when the PR head is a fork.
- `hack/list-missing-sources.sh`: reads the pinned version by parsing the Dockerfile ARG defaults; `sources.yaml` is only walked for the `version_arg` mapping.
- `hack/gen-components.sh`: dropped the `sources.yaml` `version` branch and the render fallback for the worktree path. Cached-package versions come from the Dockerfile ARG defaults; the `sources.yaml` `version_arg` -> pkg map is used purely to keep the emitted component name matching the pkg name (`libiconv`, not `iconv`; `linux`, not `kernel`). The git-ref path keeps the extract-and-render fallback so per-tag snapshots for older historical tags still generate.
- `.github/workflows/populate-sources.yml`: the `discover` and per-pkg metadata steps read the pinned version from the Dockerfile ARG default via the `version_arg` named in `sources.yaml`.
- `Makefile`: dropped the `Dockerfile:` and `render` targets and the `rm -f Dockerfile` in `clean`. `KERNEL_VERSION` / `DWARVES_VERSION` Makefile vars are grepped out of the Dockerfile ARG defaults so they no longer depend on python3+PyYAML.
- `.github/workflows/PR_multiarch.yml`, `PR_riscv64.yml`: kernel-config check reads `KERNEL_VERSION` from the Dockerfile ARG.
- `tests/render-fork-sources.sh`: rewritten around the committed Dockerfile (snapshot / restore between runs); tests the three upstream-mode branches (whole-file, restricted list, empty list) and the trusted no-op path.
- Comment fixups: `s/Dockerfile.tmpl/Dockerfile/` in a few workflow and `sources.yaml` comments.

## Bump workflow after this lands

1. Edit `Dockerfile` line `ARG <PKG>_VERSION=<new>`.
2. Edit `sources.yaml` `<pkg>.sha256` to match the new tarball.
3. Push. `populate-sources.yml` publishes the new `ghcr.io/kairos-io/hadron-sources/<pkg>:<new>` image; downstream builds pull it.

`updatecli` still walks `updatecli.d/*.yaml` and now writes back to the Dockerfile again, which is where it was pointed all along.

## Fork PRs

Fork PRs cannot publish source-cache images, so a bump to a version whose cache tag does not yet exist would fail before compilation. The slimmed `hack/render.sh` (invoked by the `render-dockerfile` composite action) still runs the FROM-line rewrite for fork PRs, replacing only the missing cache tags with checksum-verifying upstream download stages. Trusted builds skip the composite entirely. `tests/render-fork-sources.sh` covers all four paths.

## Follow-ups outside this PR

- #582 (autobumper writes bumps to `sources.yaml`) becomes obsolete; can be closed once this lands.
- If the fork-PR helper feels like scope creep worth killing, the follow-up is a separate flow to publish fork-cache images.
title: Commit the Dockerfile as the single source of truth for pinned versions

author: itxaka-agent
body:
PR builds barely hit cache even for trivial changes. On PR #594 (a
react bump that touches nothing the container build sees) toolchain-amd64
came back with 182 of 924 steps cached (~16%), container-amd64 with
570/796 (~42%), hadron-bios-amd64 cloud/no-fips with 399/1245 (~24%).
On that PR we should be seeing ~99%.

The cause is that amd64 and arm64 only wrote 3-4 monolithic quay tags
per arch — `toolchain-<arch>`, `container-<arch>`,
`bios-<kernel>-<fips>-<arch>`, `trusted-<kernel>-<arch>` — each
`mode=max` for its `--target` and packing 100+ intermediate stages
under a single OCI manifest. At the end of a ~60 minute main build
the whole thing has to push in one shot, and we deliberately keep
`ignore-error=true` on cache-to so a quay flake doesn't red main. The
side effect is that a truncated or failed push is swallowed, the next
PR imports a partial manifest, and buildkit re-runs everything past
whatever survived — usually from mid-toolchain.

This mirrors the per-stage cache layout that PR_riscv64.yml and the
riscv64 half of build-multiarch-images.yml already use. New jobs per
arch (amd64 and arm64): stage0, stage1 (`stage1-merge`), rsync, cmake,
kernel (matrix over cloud and default, `kernel-misc`), systemd and
python (`python-build`). Each writes its own small tag. The downstream
jobs (toolchain, container, hadron-bios, hadron-trusted,
hadron-grub-arm64) grew a cache-from list that pulls every upstream
stage tag before falling back to their own aggregate tag.

The PR pipeline is the same shape with `pr-<num>-<stage>-<arch>` tags
gated on `PR_CACHE_WRITE`. pr-cache-cleanup.yml already matches
`pr-<num>-*` so nothing there needs changing. `ignore-error=true`
stays on cache-to.

Runner cost: main peak per arch goes from 3 to 7 concurrent
oracle-vm-32cpu-128gb runners, same on PR. riscv64 is untouched
because it already looks like this.
title: ci: split buildx cache per stage on amd64 and arm64

author: ci-robbot
body:
Fixes kairos-io/kairos#4564.

Five of the last 40 `PR_multiarch` runs lost a job to `Install Go` before a
single test ran, always after burning exactly 5m00s:

| run | job |
| --- | --- |
| [34314852826](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/actions/runs/34314852826) | reset tests (FIPS) |
| [34294143535](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/actions/runs/34294143535) | reset tests (FIPS) |
| [34162208109](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/actions/runs/34162208109) | acceptance tests |
| [34141532218](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/actions/runs/34141532218) | acceptance tests (FIPS) |
| [33888029300](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/actions/runs/33888029300) | reset tests (FIPS) |

Exactly 5m00s is the step's own `timeout-minutes: 5`, so this is not the
toolchain download. That comes from the runner tool cache in seconds. The
rest of the step is `setup-go` restoring a ~305 MB dependency cache, and on
run 34314852826 it was at 87.8% moving at 0.9 MB/s when the cap fired.

## The change

Per @Itxaka's review: the workers cap at 100 Mb/s and a congested one is not
going to get through the image pulls later either, so the right move is to
give up early rather than to wait longer.

I sampled the step across the last 12 `PR_multiarch` runs, 92 executions of
`Install Go` in total, and the split is clean:

| | duration |
| --- | --- |
| median (91 successes) | 17s |
| p90 | 41s |
| slowest healthy | 52s |
| congested outliers | 277s (passed), 300s (timed out) |

Nothing healthy comes near a minute. So the six active `setup-go` steps drop
from `timeout-minutes: 5` to `2`, with the numbers recorded at each so the
value is not re-guessed later.

At two minutes a healthy restore keeps 2.3x headroom over the slowest one
observed, and a doomed job gives back three minutes of runner time. The cost
is the 277s case: that job did eventually pass, and now it would not. That
looks like the right trade, since it was already 5x slower than any healthy
run and the same congestion had four other jobs failing outright.

Verified the six edits all land inside `actions/setup-go` steps by parsing
the workflow and walking `jobs[*].steps[*]` (`container-amd64`,
`container-arm64`, `hadron-bios-amd64`, `tests-bios-amd64`,
`tests-trusted-amd64`, `tests-bios-fips-amd64`), which covers every job
observed failing. The commented-out block further down is left untouched.

## What I did not do

The 305 MB cache itself is the better question and I have left it alone.
`tests/go.mod` is a small Ginkgo suite with 95 modules in `go.sum`, so most
of that is `~/.cache/go-build`, not the module set. Caching only
`~/go/pkg/mod` would shrink the restore a lot, at the cost of recompiling the
test binary in every job. That wants a benchmark on the ARC runners, so it is
written up in #4564 rather than guessed at.
title: fix(ci): fail a congested setup-go cache restore fast

author: ci-robbot
body:
Closes kairos-io/kairos#4559.

## The bug

`Dockerfile.tmpl` declares the cap once, before the first `FROM`, and uses it in 218 places. A global `ARG` is only a default; a stage has to re-declare it to bring it into scope. `JOBS` is re-declared in 115 stages, `MAX_LOAD` in none, so every one of those commands ran as `make -s -j16 -l`, and GNU make reads a bare `-l` as *removing* a previous load limit.

## The change

- `ARG MAX_LOAD` next to every `ARG JOBS`, so the two share one scope. That also covers the stages that use the flag without declaring either (`util-linux`, `kernel-modules`); they inherit from `bash` and `kernel-build` exactly as they already inherit `JOBS`.
- `${MAX_LOAD:+-l${MAX_LOAD}}` instead of `-l${MAX_LOAD}`, so the flag is omitted when no cap is set instead of being passed bare.
- The global default becomes empty rather than `32`.

## Why the default is empty

The issue offered three options and asked for a decision. This is none of them, because all three needed a benchmark I cannot run: turning a cap on for the first time across a build where buildkit already runs many stages concurrently at `-j16` could throttle the ARC runners, and dropping the knob throws away the ability to find out.

Empty gives the honest version of today's behaviour, no flag at all rather than one that clobbers limits, and makes `--build-arg MAX_LOAD=32` work for the first time. Whoever owns the runners can then measure option 1 without another PR to the Dockerfile.

## Verification

No docker on this box, so I checked the two substitution layers directly with buildkit's own packages (`frontend/dockerfile/parser`, `instructions`, `shell`) plus a real `envsubst`, resolving each stage's ARG scope through its `FROM` chain and expanding every affected `RUN`:

| Dockerfile | build arg | make commands | bare `-l` | `-lN` |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `main` | default | 129 | 218 | 0 |
| `main` | `MAX_LOAD=32` | 129 | 218 | 0 |
| this PR | default | 129 | 0 | 0 |
| this PR | `MAX_LOAD=32` | 129 | 0 | 218 |

The second row is the part worth reading twice: on `main` the build arg is completely inert, setting it changes nothing.

Two other things I confirmed rather than assumed:

- `shell.Lex` with `SkipUnsetEnv` (how buildkit dispatches `RUN`) reproduces the issue's log line exactly, `make -s -j16 -l${MAX_LOAD}`, with `JOBS` resolved and `MAX_LOAD` left literal in the same command. The new form is safe in both layers: buildkit expands it when `MAX_LOAD` is in scope, and `/bin/sh` expands it correctly if it ever passes through.
- `envsubst` leaves `${MAX_LOAD:+-l${MAX_LOAD}}` untouched, so `hack/render.sh` is unaffected. Rendering both templates against `sources.yaml` gives byte-identical output apart from the `MAX_LOAD` lines and the comment, same three expected unresolved placeholders (`BASH_VERSION`, `MUSSEL_VERSION`, `SBAT_DISTRO_VERSION`) before and after.

## Note for a follow-up

The two remaining bare `-l` in the tree are `./mussel ... -k -l -o -p -s` and `attr -l /bin/bash`. Both are correct.
title: fix(make): stop passing a bare -l, and put MAX_LOAD in scope

author: ci-robbot
body:
## What

Patch shim 16.1's Makefile so the rule that builds `libgnuefi.a` and
`libefi.a` is a grouped target (`&:`) instead of two plain targets sharing
a recipe.

## Why

`hadron-bios-amd64 (cloud, fips)` failed on `main` in
[run 34233932920](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/actions/runs/34233932920)
while its seven sibling legs passed:

```
/usr/lib/gcc/.../ar: creating libgnuefi.a
/usr/lib/gcc/.../ar: libgnuefi.a: file format not recognized
make[2]: *** [gnu-efi/gnuefi/Makefile:56: libgnuefi.a] Error 1
make: *** [Makefile:172: gnu-efi/x86_64/lib/libefi.a] Error 2
```

shim's Makefile has:

```make
gnu-efi/$(ARCH_GNUEFI)/gnuefi/libgnuefi.a gnu-efi/$(ARCH_GNUEFI)/lib/libefi.a:
	$(MAKE) -C gnu-efi ... lib gnuefi inc
```

Two file names before a single `:` is not one recipe producing two files.
GNU make reads it as two independent rules that happen to share a recipe.
We build with `-j16`, both rules are eligible at once, so make runs the
gnu-efi sub-make twice in parallel in the same directory and the two `ar`
processes write the same archive.

The double run is not occasional. It happens on every build and the logs
show it plainly. In the failing amd64 leg, one `ar` adds each object to
`libefi.a`, and 150ms later a second `ar` replaces every one of them:

```
2.226 ar: creating libefi.a
2.226 a - boxdraw.o      <- first sub-make
...
2.372 r - boxdraw.o      <- second sub-make, replacing
```

The green `hadron-bios-arm64 (cloud, fips)` leg in the same run shows the
identical `a -` then `r -` pair. It just won the race on `libgnuefi.a`.
So this is a latent flake that reds a random leg now and then, and it also
does the whole gnu-efi build twice on every successful build.

## How

`&:` declares a grouped target: one recipe that produces every file listed,
scheduled once. It needs GNU make 4.3 or newer and hadron pins 4.4.1
(`MAKE_VERSION=4.4.1`).

The patch goes through the existing `patches/` mechanism rather than another
`sed -i`, so a shim bump makes the build fail loudly instead of silently
dropping the fix.

shim's `main` branch still has the plain `:`, so the patch stays until
upstream takes it. Happy to send it to rhboot/shim if you want that first.

## Verification

- The patch applies cleanly to the pinned tarball. I downloaded
  `shim-16.1.tar.bz2`, confirmed its sha256 is
  `46319cd228d8f2c06c744241c0f342412329a7c630436fce7f82cf6936b1d603` (the
  value in `sources.yaml`), applied the patch to it, and checked the
  resulting rule reads `... libefi.a &:`.
- I cannot build hadron on this box (no docker), so CI is the real check.
  What to look for in the shim stage of a green run: the `a - <obj>` lines
  should no longer be followed by a matching set of `r - <obj>` lines, and
  the stage should get slightly faster.
title: fix(shim): stop the ar race in the gnu-efi build

author: ci-robbot
body:
Fixes the base-image half of kairos-io/kairos#4290. Design agreed with @Itxaka on the issue.

## The problem

`/usr/lib/firmware` was a symlink into `/usr/local/lib/firmware`:

```
RUN rm -rf /lib/firmware && \
    mkdir -p /usr/local/lib/firmware && \
    ln -s /usr/local/lib/firmware /lib/firmware
```

`/usr/local` is where `COS_PERSISTENT` gets mounted (`VOLUMES` in `00_rootfs.yaml`). Unlike the other two layout mechanisms, that one has no lower layer:

| env key | mechanism | image content underneath |
| --- | --- | --- |
| `VOLUMES` (`/usr/local`) | plain rw device mount | **shadowed permanently** |
| `PERSISTENT_STATE_PATHS` | bind from `/usr/local/.state/*.bind`, rsynced up first | preserved |
| `RW_PATHS` | tmpfs overlay, image dir as lowerdir | preserved |

So on an installed node every firmware blob baked into the image sat behind an empty partition. That is the symptom reported in #4290.

## The change

```
RUN mkdir -p /usr/lib/firmware /usr/local/lib/firmware && \
    ln -s /usr/local/lib/firmware /usr/lib/firmware/updates
```

Image blobs stay in the real directory `/usr/lib/firmware`, on the read-only rootfs where the persistent mount cannot reach them. The persistent partition becomes the *override* directory, `/usr/lib/firmware/updates`.

**Precedence comes from the kernel, not from us.** `fw_path[]` in `drivers/base/firmware_loader/main.c`:

```c
static const char * const fw_path[] = {
	fw_path_para,
	"/lib/firmware/updates/" UTS_RELEASE,
	"/lib/firmware/updates",
	"/lib/firmware/" UTS_RELEASE,
	"/lib/firmware"
};
```

`/lib/firmware/updates` is searched before `/lib/firmware`, with nothing set. The loop skips an unset entry and treats a failed open as "try the next path". So:

- **Nothing on the kernel cmdline.** No `firmware_class.path=`, so a user replacing the whole cmdline cannot break it, and UKI is unaffected. This also sidesteps a real inconsistency in our own configs: `CONFIG_FW_LOADER=m` on `cloud.config` and `cloud-arm64.config` but `=y` on riscv64, which would have made `firmware_class.path=` a module parameter on some arches and a boot parameter on others.
- **Nothing in the kernel config.** There is no Kconfig for the runtime search path. `CONFIG_EXTRA_FIRMWARE`/`_DIR` only control blobs linked into vmlinux at build time.
- **Persistent not mounted** (live media, initramfs, first boot): the symlink dangles, that path yields `-ENOENT`, the loop falls through to `/lib/firmware` and the image blobs load. The old layout could not do this at all.
- **Persistent mounted with an operator blob in it**: `updates` resolves first and the operator blob wins.

`/lib/firmware` resolves through the `/lib -> usr/lib` symlink the skeleton already creates, and the loader reads via `kernel_read_file_from_path_initns`, so it is ordinary path resolution in init's mount namespace: it follows the symlink and it sees sysext overlays.

## Why the directory has to be real

Baked-in firmware and sysext firmware both have to work, sometimes on the same image. A symlink at `/usr/lib/firmware` prevents that: overlayfs merges a directory in an upper layer with a directory in a lower one, but an **upper directory replaces a lower symlink outright**. Under the old layout a sysext shipping `usr/lib/firmware/` *replaced* the base blobs instead of adding to them. With a real directory the two merge.

The writable-directory concern raised on the issue does not apply: `systemd-sysext` mounts a read-only overlay over `/usr`, and the only thing that must be writable is where the extension images live. `/var/lib/extensions` and `/var/lib/confexts` are already in `PERSISTENT_STATE_PATHS`.

## Tests

`assertFirmwareLayout` in the acceptance suite, called from "passes checks", so it runs on a real installed node with the persistent partition mounted:

- `/usr/lib/firmware` is a directory and not a symlink.
- `stat -c %d /usr/lib/firmware` differs from `stat -c %d /usr/local`, i.e. the firmware directory is not backed by the persistent device. This is the regression assertion: it fails on the old layout.
- `readlink /usr/lib/firmware/updates` is `/usr/local/lib/firmware`, and a file written to `/usr/local/lib/firmware` is readable through `/lib/firmware/updates/`, which is the exact path the kernel opens.

Ran `go vet ./...` and `gofmt -l .` in `tests/` (clean). The acceptance suite itself needs QEMU and a built image, so CI runs it.

**What I could not verify here:** no container runtime, no root and no unprivileged user namespaces on this machine, so the `fw_path[]` ordering and the overlayfs merge behaviour above are read from the kernel and overlayfs sources rather than observed on a booted machine. The acceptance assertion covers the mount-shadowing half on CI. The `updates`-before-`/lib/firmware` ordering is worth one confirmation on hardware that actually requests firmware; @tbrasser offered a three-node bare-metal fleet on #4290 (Realtek/Aquantia, gfx1151, MT7925).

## Ordering

This PR is safe on its own and must land first, because the composers copy image roots:

1. **This PR.** Firmware images built with today's `DESTDIR=/usr/local/lib/firmware` still copy into `/usr/local/lib/firmware`, which now means "override" instead of "baked in". Nothing breaks.
2. `kairos-io/hadron-firmware`: point `DESTDIR` at `/usr/lib/firmware` so the published layers and sysexts land in the baked-in location.
3. `kairos-io/AuroraBoot`: drop the now-dead `if [ -L /usr/local/lib/firmware ]` guard in `hadronContent.ts`, once a base with this layout is released. The guard becomes a no-op here, not wrong, so it has to stay until then.

/cc @Itxaka
title: fix(firmware): keep image blobs out of the persistent mount

author: mauro-agent
body:
Follow-up to kairos-io/hadron#572 (merged) and the un-split riscv64 pipeline. Lifts the `if: ${{ false }}` gate on `populate-sources` and `stage0` in `PR_riscv64.yml` only, unblocking the full `stage0 -> stage1 -> rsync -> ... -> hadron-bios` chain for this PR's own CI run.

**Purpose**: get one real CI run of the un-split, x86+QEMU-only riscv64 pipeline, and a warm-cache timing number — the evidence needed before proposing re-enabling riscv64 CI to kairos-io maintainers.

**Scope, deliberately narrow**:
- `check-kernel-configs` stays gated off; it's unrelated to the build chain.
- `build-multiarch-images.yml`'s riscv64 jobs (release path) are untouched.
- This is a one-shot measurement, not a decision to keep riscv64 CI on. Revert after reading the timing, or open a follow-up to remove the gates for good if the number looks good.

Draft, per repo convention; not proposing merge yet.
title: ci(riscv64): lift the populate-sources/stage0 gate for one timing run

notes:
# Hadron v0.5.2

Released 2026-09-09 · 86 commits since [v0.5.1](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/releases/tag/v0.5.1) (2026-07-09) · [full compare](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/compare/v0.5.1...v0.5.2)

## Highlights

- **Firmware landing site fixed.** Image blobs now ship at `/usr/lib/firmware` (a real directory), and `/usr/lib/firmware/updates → /usr/local/lib/firmware` gives operators the override slot without needing anything on the kernel cmdline. The kernel's own `fw_path[]` searches `updates/` first, so overrides always win over baked-in blobs. Nodes that used to boot with an empty firmware tree because COS_PERSISTENT shadowed the shipped blobs no longer do. ([#581](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/pull/581), fixes [kairos-io/kairos#4290](https://github.com/kairos-io/kairos/issues/4290))
- **Real `less` replaces the busybox applet.** Hadron images now ship upstream `less-704` linked against a narrow ncurses runtime (libtinfo + 13 terminfo entries). The busybox `LESS` applet is disabled so there is one pager on the system. Net cost is around ~180 KB per image variant after trimming man pages and headers. ([#587](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/pull/587), [#590](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/pull/590))
- **Kernel BTF is on.** `CONFIG_DEBUG_INFO_BTF` is enabled everywhere (including riscv64, where `DEBUG_KERNEL` had to be forced so olddefconfig couldn't silently strip BTF back off), and the build image carries `dwarves`/`pahole` as required. bpftrace, bpftool and CO-RE-based observability tools now work out of the box. ([#512](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/pull/512), [#530](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/pull/530))
- **`shim` no longer races itself.** The GNU EFI build had two Makefile targets sharing a recipe under `make -j`, occasionally producing the "ar: file format not recognized" flake in CI. Grouped-target syntax (`&:`, GNU make ≥4.3) closes the race. ([#592](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/pull/592))
- **`getent` and `nslookup` are in the base image.** Two small but frequently-missed tools for anyone debugging DNS or NSS on a running node. ([#523](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/pull/523))
- **CI source-fetch stops depending on `ttl.sh` and bare `kernel.org`.** The build now pulls the kernel and libcap tarballs from `cdn.kernel.org`, and every package downloader stage is backed by a per-package source cache on ghcr populated from a matrix over `sources.yaml`. Fork PRs also fetch sources directly instead of through the cache path they can't write to. Fewer flaky mirror timeouts, faster warm builds, and the arm64/amd64 image handoff between jobs is now a tarball artifact instead of a `ttl.sh` push. ([#566](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/pull/566), [#567](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/pull/567), [#580](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/pull/580), plus the source-cache series `3fed87f..dc4d3ef`)

## Changes

### Base image / userland

- `less-704` replaces the busybox applet, with a narrow ncurses runtime for terminfo ([#587](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/pull/587)).
- Busybox `CONFIG_LESS` (and every `CONFIG_FEATURE_LESS_*`) disabled so there is exactly one `less` on the system ([#590](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/pull/590)).
- Firmware layout fixed: `/usr/lib/firmware` real dir + `/usr/lib/firmware/updates → /usr/local/lib/firmware` for overrides ([#581](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/pull/581)).
- `getent` and `nslookup` added to the base image ([#523](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/pull/523)).
- Removed the redundant system-openssh install that was segfaulting on MLDSA44 keys under FIPS OpenSSL ([#511](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/pull/511)).
- sshd drop-in precedence fixed so hadron's `sshd_config.d/` overrides win where the upstream defaults are stricter ([#571](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/pull/571)).

### Kernel

- BTF support enabled across every variant, with the toolchain (`dwarves`/`pahole`) added to the `update-kernel-configs` stage ([#512](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/pull/512), [#527](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/pull/527)).
- `DEBUG_KERNEL=y` on `cloud-riscv64` so `olddefconfig` doesn't silently drop BTF back off ([#530](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/pull/530)).
- Regular kernel bumps via the autobumper.

### Build system

- Shim's gnu-efi build converted to grouped-target Makefile syntax, killing the intermittent `ar: file format not recognized` under `make -j` ([#592](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/pull/592)).
- `make` split into a local base build tag and a separate published `PULL_IMAGE_NAME`, so a local `make build-hadron` no longer collides with the published `ghcr.io/kairos-io/hadron:main` tag ([#589](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/pull/589)).
- `stage0` pre-stages musl for mussel; the toolchain build no longer hits `musl.libc.org` on every run ([#578](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/pull/578)).
- `nfs-utils` linkage fixed by patching the exportfs header rather than enabling nfsdctl ([`9c4ade8`](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/commit/9c4ade8)); `lvm2`'s parallel-install race on `dmstats` symlinks fixed ([`d348d7e`](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/commit/d348d7e)); autobumper matrix jobs no longer race each other on the fork ([#591](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/pull/591)).

### Dependency bumps

- shadow → 4.20.2 (upstreamed musl patch dropped) ([#584](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/pull/584)).
- busybox → 1.38.0 (minimal.config regenerated) ([#586](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/pull/586)).
- nfs-utils → 2.9.2, plus a shadow-for-musl patch ([`1be9ac3`](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/commit/1be9ac3)).
- Regular autobump traffic for `gawk`, `pkgconfig`, `cmake`, `libffi`, `openssh`, `findutils`, `perl`, `tpm2_tss`, `libucontext`, `open_iscsi`, `cryptsetup`, `systemd`, `sqlite3`, `binutils`, `multipath`, `dracut`, `pax_utils`, `python`, `libkcapi`, `lvm2`, `pkgconfig`.

### CI / infrastructure

- Fork PRs now fetch sources directly instead of through the cache write path they can't reach ([#580](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/pull/580)).
- amd64 and trusted build chains moved off `ttl.sh`; arm64 image handoff between jobs is now a tarball artifact ([#566](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/pull/566), [#567](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/pull/567)).
- hadron's riscv64 pipeline unified and moved off the native runner ([#572](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/pull/572)).
- Kernel and libcap tarballs fetched from `cdn.kernel.org` instead of the bare cgit snapshot ([`3fed87f`](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/commit/3fed87f), [`1b6ff27`](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/commit/1b6ff27)).
- Per-package source cache on ghcr, populated from a matrix over `sources.yaml`, with sha-verified fallback URLs and pre-filtering to skip the matrix on a warm cache ([`57e57dd..dc4d3ef`](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/compare/57e57dd...dc4d3ef)).
- `gen-components` auto-renders the Dockerfile from the template when it's absent ([`f008b67`](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/commit/f008b67)).

### Tests

- Extension install coverage added for the non-UKI recovery boot path ([#565](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/pull/565)).
- Component versions report renders the rendered Dockerfile on the amd64 job ([`fb5b34b`](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/commit/fb5b34b)).

### Documentation

- Issue reporting pointed at `kairos-io/kairos` so the tracker doesn't split ([#575](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/pull/575)).
- riscv64: recorded that `preset-all` no longer crashes under QEMU ([#564](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/pull/564)).
- Docs page rebuilds every two hours so external firmware/layers data stays fresh ([#524](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/pull/524)).
- Layer sysext artifacts now render on the components page ([#568](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/pull/568)).
- LICENSE added ([`7b242bb`](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/commit/7b242bb)).

## Contributors

Thanks to [@Itxaka](https://github.com/Itxaka), [@jimmykarily](https://github.com/jimmykarily), [@mudler](https://github.com/mudler), [@mauromorales](https://github.com/mauromorales), and the automation cohort: [@ci-robbot](https://github.com/ci-robbot), [@mudler-agent](https://github.com/mudler-agent), [@mauro-agent](https://github.com/mauro-agent), [@itxaka-agent](https://github.com/itxaka-agent), [@Copilot](https://github.com/Copilot), and Renovate.

# v0.2.0 - The Lucky Seven Release

### New Features

#### Linux Kernel 7.0

Major kernel upgrade to the Linux 7.0 series. This release ships with kernel 7.0.6, bringing improved hardware 
support, performance optimizations, and the latest upstream features.

#### DirtyFrag CVE Mitigation

Proactive mitigation for the DirtyFrag vulnerability (CVE pending). The nf_defrag_ipv4 and nf_defrag_ipv6 kernel 
modules are now blocklisted by default to prevent exploitation until a patched kernel is available upstream.

#### Thor GPU Support

New example Dockerfile and documentation for building Hadron images with Thor GPU accelerator support, enabling 
AI/ML workloads on Thor-based systems.

#### RISC-V Multi-Architecture Manifests

RISC-V (riscv64) images are now included in multi-architecture container manifests, allowing seamless pulls on 
RISC-V hardware without specifying the architecture explicitly.

#### ARM64 Nvidia Kernel Support

Additional kernel configuration options enabled for ARM64 to support Nvidia GPU drivers, expanding GPU compute 
capabilities on ARM-based systems.

#### GRUB SMBIOS Support

GRUB bootloader now includes SMBIOS module support, enabling system identification and hardware inventory at boot 
time.

#### Improved Build Flexibility

The Dockerfile now supports parameterized base images and tags, making it easier to customize builds and integrate 
with different base image sources.

### New Features                                                                                                    
                  
#### RISC-V (riscv64) Architecture Support                                                                          
Full riscv64 architecture support added. Includes cross-compilation toolchain, default and cloud kernel configs,
GRUB EFI, QEMU emulation, and a dedicated CI workflow running on RISE RISC-V runners.                           
                                                                                                                    
#### Intel TDX Host Support
Default kernel now includes Intel Trusted Domain Extensions (TDX) host support for confidential computing           
deployments.                                                                                             
                                                                                                                    
#### Nvidia Extension Build Pipeline
New CI workflow for building Nvidia driver extensions, enabling GPU workloads on Hadron-based systems.              
                                                                                                      
#### Parallel Source Downloads                                                                                      
Dockerfile refactored so all ~60 source packages download in parallel independent stages. Significant reduction in
build time for clean builds.

author: kkaempf
body:
Currently Elemental can only be used to provision machines for _downstream_ clusters.
Installation depends on an existing (Rancher) management cluster where `elemental-operator` is running.

This issue asks for a "seed installation" concept. Where we start with a (bare metal) machine (resp. VM / cloud image), install Elemental and then Rancher on top.

Bonus points if we find a way to install elemental-operator on this Rancher instance and self-manage the machine.
title: Seed installation - first Elemental, then Rancher

author: leptitchriss
body:
**Environment.** Harvester v1.8.2 (bundled elemental `1.1.8+gaf99ad9`), Lenovo ThinkStation P620 (BIOS S07KT24A), UEFI, unattended install over PXE. The machine had a previous elemental-based install whose standard boot entry had already been removed.

**Symptom.** `elemental install` fails after partitioning:

```
1 error occurred:
* remove /sys/firmware/efi/efivars/lBoot0006-146b234d-4052-4e07-b326-11220f8e1fe8: invalid argument
```

`lBoot0006` is not a boot entry. It is a Lenovo vendor variable under GUID `146b234d-4052-4e07-b326-11220f8e1fe8`: this firmware keeps an `lBoot####` twin of every `Boot####`, with attributes `0x6` (BootService + Runtime, **not** NonVolatile) — volatile mirrors it regenerates each boot, which is why it refuses to delete them (`chattr -i` + `rm` → `EINVAL` as well). Their contents parse as load options, so the twin of a former `elemental-shim` entry carries that description.

**Cause.** The stale-entry cleanup matches every variable whose *name contains* `Boot[0-9a-fA-F]{4}`, under any GUID:

- v1.1.8: `pkg/utils/grub.go` `ClearBootEntry` — `regexp.MustCompile(`Boot[0-9a-fA-F]{4}`).MatchString(v.Name)` over `efilib.ListVariables()`, no check of `v.GUID`
- main (f04a36c): `pkg/bootloader/grub.go` `clearEntry`, same pattern

The vendor twin matches, its description equals the entry name, the delete fails, and the whole install aborts.

**Expected.** Only names matching `^Boot[0-9a-fA-F]{4}$` under `efi.GlobalVariable` should be candidates. Arguably a failed delete of a *stale* entry should also not abort the install, since the entry that matters is the one created afterwards.

**Reproduce.** On a Lenovo UEFI machine that has had an elemental install before: `ls /sys/firmware/efi/efivars | grep -i 'boot[0-9a-f]\{4\}'` shows `lBoot####-146b234d-…` entries; run `elemental install`.

**Workaround that worked.** Before the install, from the live system: `mount --bind /dev/null /sys/firmware/efi/efivars/lBoot0006-146b234d-4052-4e07-b326-11220f8e1fe8`. The variable then fails to parse as a load option, the cleanup skips it, and the real entry is created normally. Remounting efivars read-only does not help on 1.1.8 (no `WithGrubAutoDisableBootEntry` there): the error just becomes `read-only file system`.
title: install: boot-entry cleanup matches any EFI variable containing "Boot####" under any GUID, and aborts on Lenovo's undeletable lBoot#### mirrors

Jul 11 00:56:49 node0 elemental[1581]: INFO[2025-07-11T00:56:49Z] Processing stage step 'testtest-boot-stage-from-99_test_yaml'. ( commands: 1, files: 0, ... )
Jul 11 00:56:49 node0 elemental[1581]: INFO[2025-07-11T00:56:49Z] Processing stage step 'testtest-boot-stage-from-00_test_yaml'. ( commands: 1, files: 0, ... )

      commands:

    - name: "testtest-boot-stage-from-00_test_yaml"
      commands:

EOF

cat <<EOF > /oem/99_test.yaml
stages:
  rootfs:
    - name: "testtest-rootfs-stage-from-99_test_yaml"
      commands:
      - cat /sysroot/etc/passwd
  initramfs:
    - name: "testtest-initramfs-stage-from-99_test_yaml"
      commands:
      - cat /etc/passwd
  fs:
    - name: "testtest-fs-stage-from-99_test_yaml"
      commands:

    - name: "testtest-boot-stage-from-99_test_yaml"

author: leptitchriss
body:
The stale boot entry cleanup matched any EFI variable whose name contains "Boot####", under any GUID. Some firmware keeps vendor variables of that shape whose contents also parse as load options (Lenovo mirrors every Boot#### as lBoot#### under its own GUID) and refuses to delete them, so a previous install's entry made every later install fail with "invalid argument" on the vendor variable.

This restricts the candidates to names matching `^Boot[0-9a-fA-F]{4}$` under the EFI global variable GUID, which is what a boot entry is. The behaviour is covered with the mock variables through an `export_test.go` shim, so the method stays unexported. The new spec plants a vendor-GUID twin of a stale entry and an unrelated global entry beside it and checks that only the stale entry is removed; it fails on the previous logic.

Fixes #2433
title: Only consider global Boot#### variables when clearing stale entries

## Release 2.1.1

This major new release of Elemental Toolkit includes support for BTRFS and Snapper based snapshots as a key feature. This encompasses a major refactor of how OS images are managed and laid out into disk. While it is possible to **upgrade** from an old image to a new image based on Elemental toolkit v2, it is not possible to **downgrade**.

cOS-toolkit is an experimental framework to build, ship, release and maintain Linux Derivatives as Container images. 

By default cOS comes with an immutable-rootfs setup. cOS supports to upgrade specifying directly docker image references and with standard upgrade channel.

In this release:

- Gained support for upgrades with signed images with mtree #251 
- Added SELinux support #135 
- PoC for building cloud images - we have a new make target (`make raw_disk`) to build unprivileged disks that can be booted in AWS.
- We have introduced a mechanism to have the recovery partition also supplied as a separated squashfs file which is being used by the Cloud images. We also gained support to optionally supply a different image being used for the recovery partition. 
- Cloud-init tool had various updates:  support for partitioning, cloud data sources and more fine-grained user control ( https://github.com/rancher-sandbox/cOS-toolkit/blob/master/docs/derivatives_featureset.md#configuration-reference )

Luet version used for building packages: `0.16.7`

## Bug Report
Similar to Ubuntu Kernel https://bugs.launchpad.net/ubuntu/+source/linux/+bug/2166680
Current TalosOS kernel rbd module does not support the new longer CephX keys
Related to introduced longer key length in https://docs.ceph.com/en/latest/security/CVE-2025-30156/

### Description
This affects blocks any Kubernetes deployment that connects to Ceph CSI through the default mounter krbd and wants to mitigate ciritical CVE-2025-30156 by using the longer CephX keys

The two current options to connect to Ceph from a Talos K8s are
- A: Use a non stable mounter. Use userspace rbd client `nbd-rbd` which is [not yet stable in Ceph CSI (alpha)](https://github.com/ceph/ceph-csi/blob/devel/docs/design/proposals/rbd-nbd.md#overview) and [not recommended in production usage in Rook](https://rook.io/docs/rook/latest/CRDs/Cluster/ceph-cluster-crd/#network-configuration-settings) but has a patch to use `aes256k` CephX keys
- B: Continue using the stable mounter `krbd` with `aes` but being vulnerable to the [critical CVE](https://docs.ceph.com/en/latest/security/CVE-2025-30156/) 

### Logs

```bash
# kubectl describe po

author: lucndm
body:
### What happened

With workload isolation enabled, every boot shows CRI in a fail/restart
loop for ~1-3 minutes before it finally starts, leaving the node
DEGRADED (kubelet down, Node NotReady):

```
service[cri](Waiting): Error running Process(["/bin/containerd" ...]),
going to restart forever: sandbox namespace not available yet
```

### Root cause

`CRI.DependsOn` and `CRI.Runner` evaluate `sandboxd.Enabled(r)` at
different times:

1. CRI is started in the early services phase, **before** the machine
   config is loaded → `r.Config() == nil` → `sandboxd.Enabled()` is
   false → CRI gets **no dependency** on sandboxd.
2. CRI's own Condition (network, /etc files) becomes satisfiable only
   after the config is loaded. When the runner is finally created,
   `sandboxd.Enabled()` is now true → `WithSandbox(r.Sandbox)` is set →
   but sandboxd only starts later in the startEverything phase, so the
   launcher is still nil → `runInSandbox` fails → restart-forever
   (5s interval) until sandboxd publishes the launcher.

### Expected behavior

A service configured to run inside the sandbox namespace should wait for
the launcher to be published instead of failing and restart-looping.

### Environment

- Talos v1.14.0, `SecurityProfileConfig` with `workloadIsolation: true`
title: workload isolation: CRI fails its first launches with "sandbox namespace not available yet" and restart-loops every boot

author: lucndm
body:
### What happened

A Talos v1.14.0 worker node (metal, QEMU/KVM) rebooted gracefully every
~70m30s, 9+ times in a row. Every cycle: all pods killed simultaneously
(exit 255, Unknown), MachineStatusEvent REBOOTING, ordered service
shutdown, warm reboot (qemu process never restarted). The node recovered
to Ready each boot and ran fine for the next ~67 minutes.

### Root cause

The node runs an image built from a schematic containing the
qemu-guest-agent extension, but the hypervisor VM does not define the
virtio-serial guest-agent channel. As a result:

1. `ext-qemu-guest-agent` waits forever for
   `/dev/virtio-ports/org.qemu.guest_agent.0` and never leaves `Waiting`
   (this is arguably an operator footgun, but see the failure mode below).
2. `StartAllServices` waits for **all** services to be Up/Finished with
   `constants.BootTimeout` (70m).
3. The context expires → boot sequence fails with
   `error running phase 9 in boot sequence: task 1/1: failed, 1 error occurred: * context deadline exceeded`
4. The FATAL SequenceEvent is picked up by machined's event watcher →
   `handle()` → `unix.Reboot(RESTART)` → warm reboot → loop (4227s ≈
   4200s BootTimeout + boot overhead).

### Why it was so hard to diagnose

The boot error, the events ring, and dmesg contain **no mention of the
service** which never came up. The only evidence is the 15-second ticker
line buried in machined logs:

```
[talos] task startAllServices (1/1): service "ext-qemu-guest-agent" to be up/finished
```

and `talosctl services` showing one service in `Waiting` forever. It took
a full incident investigation to go from "reboots every 70m with no
trigger event in the ring" to the single stuck extension service.

### Expected behavior

The boot failure (and the FATAL sequence event, which is what operators
actually see) should **name the services which never reached Up**.

Worth discussing separately: whether an extension service that cannot
ever satisfy its condition should FATAL-reboot the node at all, or only
degrade it.

### Environment

- Talos v1.14.0, platform metal, QEMU/KVM (libvirt q35)
- Worker node; control plane on a different hypervisor without the
  extension was unaffected
title: boot: a service stuck in Waiting causes a silent FATAL reboot loop after 70m, and the error names no service

author: vooodoo10
body:
## Bug Report

### Description

`KubeletConfig` does not support the `extraMounts` field in Talos v1.14.

We are migrating an existing Talos configuration to v1.14 and have the following patch:

```yaml
apiVersion: v1alpha1
kind: KubeletConfig

extraMounts:
  - destination: /var/lib/linstor
    options:
      - bind
      - rshared
      - rw
    source: /var/lib/linstor
    type: bind
```

When validating the configuration with TOPF, the patch fails with:

```text
error decoding document v1alpha1/KubeletConfig/:
unknown keys found during decoding:
extraMounts:
    - destination: /var/lib/linstor
      options:
        - bind
        - rshared
        - rw
      source: /var/lib/linstor
      type: bind
```

The same configuration concept was previously used in our Talos configuration, but `extraMounts` is no longer accepted as a field of the standalone `KubeletConfig` document.

We need a supported way to configure kubelet `extraMounts` in Talos v1.14 while preserving the existing behavior.

### Logs

```text
time=2026-09-14T13:02:37.938+03:30 level=ERROR msg="node pre-checks" command=apply node=iaas-c01-cld-thr-az2-03 error="couldn't load patches: failed to parse patches in file /.../all/13-linstor-mount.yaml: failed to load patch at document index 0: error decoding document v1alpha1/KubeletConfig/ (line 1): unknown keys found during decoding:
extraMounts:
    - destination: /var/lib/linstor
      options:
        - bind
        - rshared
        - rw
      source: /var/lib/linstor
      type: bind"
```

### Environment

* Talos version: `v1.14.x`
* Kubernetes version: `v1.36.2`
* Platform: bare-metal / Talos Linux
* Configuration tool: TOPF
* Storage: LINSTOR

### Expected behavior

`extraMounts` should either be supported by `KubeletConfig` or there should be a documented v1.14 configuration mechanism for configuring kubelet extra mounts.

### Actual behavior

The `KubeletConfig` document is rejected because `extraMounts` is reported as an unknown field.

### Workaround

The configuration can potentially be expressed through the machine configuration:

```yaml
machine:
  kubelet:
    extraMounts:
      - destination: /var/lib/linstor
        source: /var/lib/linstor
        type: bind
        options:
          - bind
          - rshared
          - rw
```

However, clarification/documentation is needed on whether this is the intended v1.14 replacement for the previous `KubeletConfig` configuration.
title: v1.14 KubeletConfig not support extraMounts.

author: astro-stan
body:
## Feature Request

### Description

Context: https://github.com/siderolabs/talos/discussions/12132

TL;DR:

`talos upgrade` performs no validation if the chosen image is compatible with the node. To make matters worse, the `--image` option has a default argument, which upgrades the node to a "default" image. 

The "default" image is seemingly randomly chosen as it is unlikely to have the same schematic ID as the one on the node or might be an older version than what is currently installed.

An implicit upgrade to a "default" image would be unexpected for a Talos administrator, but _should_ be generally safe as it is assumed it is a reversible action due to Talos' A/B upgrades and the existence of the `talosctl rollback` command. 

However, as shown in the discussion linked above - there is an edge case. For Talos nodes with secure boot enabled, upgrading to a non-secure boot image completely bricks the node, as `systemd-boot` gets replaced. 

To recover from such situation, at the very least requires physical access and a live USB. However, if combined with TPM-encrypted partitions/disks, booting from an USB causes the node to get stuck in a "booting" state, as the TPM will refuse to unseal the keys for the partitions/disks. Thus wiping the `STATE` and `EPHEMERAL` partitions and starting fresh becomes the only option, leading to **data loss**

### Feature Request

With that in mind, I would like to suggest a few ideas on how to improve the `upgrade` command, so that you cannot accidentally shoot yourself in the foot:

- Remove the default value for the `--image` option
- Perform validation checks when upgrading and require `--force` (or something to that effect) if upgrading to an older image, from a secure boot to a non-secure boot image, or if changing image arch.
- Change the default `--image` value to be "what is currently specified in the machine config" or require `--image` to be provided if `--insecure` is used

**Bonus:** Add a "boot into maintanance mode without wiping the system disk" boot entry to the Talos ISO
title: Improve `talos upgrade` command

author: rfranlund
body:
## Bug Report

**Title:** v1.14.0: nodes booting from an SD card (SDHCI/mmc) intermittently land in maintenance mode — no settle covers mmc

### Description

Raspberry Pi 5 nodes booting Talos v1.14.0 from an SD card intermittently fail to boot into their
installed configuration and enter maintenance mode instead. `STATE` and `META` are intact on the SD card
the whole time — the node declares them missing before the mmc card has been enumerated, and by the time
the partitions appear the decision has already been made.

In a controlled series of 30 reboots across three nodes:

| node | board | reboots | maintenance mode |
|---|---|---|---|
| node-02 | Raspberry Pi 5 | 10 | **2** |
| node-03 | Raspberry Pi 5 | 10 | **2** |
| node-01 | Raspberry Pi 4 | 10 | 0 |

**4 of 20 Pi 5 boots (20 %) entered maintenance mode**, spread over both boards. The Pi 4 booted normally
10 of 10 times; see *Analysis* for why its timing leaves a large margin. An earlier, less controlled set of
reboots on one of the Pi 5 boards (reboot method not recorded) failed 5 of 7, so the rate may vary with
conditions I have not isolated.

This is the same class of bug as #14260, but for SD/mmc rather than USB. The fix for #14260
(`67ae852a`, "wait for USB settle explicitly") introduces
`internal/app/machined/pkg/controllers/block/internal/usbsettle`, which is triggered off the presence of
USB controllers, so it does not cover this path.

Applying the same machine config via `talosctl apply-config --insecure` while the node sits in
maintenance mode brings it up fully and it runs on v1.14.0 normally until the next reboot.

### Environment

- Raspberry Pi 5 Model B (BCM2712) ×2, booting from SD card (`FD4Q9 119 GiB`, UHS-I SDR104 SDXC)
  - Image Factory installer, overlay `siderolabs/sbc-raspberrypi` / `rpi_5` (sbc-raspberrypi v0.2.1)
  - Schematic `7950799b9a46e0b2959746cdcfbdd8409dbb078dc680c8e14f0ea039b28aa140`
  - SD controller: `sdhci-brcmstb` on `1000fff000.mmc`
- Raspberry Pi 4 Model B Rev 1.4 (BCM2711) ×1, same SD card model, running in UHS-I DDR50
  - Image Factory installer, schematic `6940643a90c1ca8ced2a3a248ae8d67f4959542864b80e62a5520cf4bc175337`
  - SD controller: `fe340000.mmc` (`sdhci-iproc`)
- Talos v1.14.0, kernel `6.18.48-talos` arm64, `talosctl` v1.14.0
- System disk `/dev/mmcblk0`, with `META`/`STATE`/`EPHEMERAL` on `p4`/`p5`/`p6`

### Method

- Each node was drained, then rebooted 10 times with `talosctl reboot --mode powercycle` (a full firmware
  reboot, bypassing kexec).
- A boot was counted as maintenance mode when the node answered only on the maintenance API
  (`talosctl dmesg --insecure` succeeding). Every such boot — and no other — logged
  `entering maintenance service`.
- After each boot the full kernel log was captured in a single `talosctl dmesg` read (`--insecure` for
  maintenance-mode boots), and a failed boot was recovered with `apply-config --insecure`. The next reboot
  waited until kubelet (and on the control-plane node, etcd on all members) was healthy.
- **All times below are milliseconds since `Booting Linux`, taken from a single read per boot.** These
  boards have no RTC and the wall clock jumps when time sync lands, so absolute timestamps from different
  reads are not comparable. Intervals within one read are.

### The deciding condition

The outcome turns on one comparison: **do `mmcblk0`'s partitions appear before `block.VolumeManagerController`
decides `META`/`STATE` are missing?** On every failing boot that decision was logged 17–98 ms after
`waitForUdevd` returned. Measuring when the partitions appear relative to `waitForUdevd` returning therefore
separates all 30 boots cleanly:

| partitions appeared, relative to `waitForUdevd` done | boots | outcome |
|---|---|---|
| 1276 to 910 ms **before** (Pi 4) | 10 | all normal |
| 248 ms before to 19 ms **after** (Pi 5) | 16 | all normal |
| 116 to 384 ms **after** (Pi 5) | 4 | all maintenance mode |

Per boot, Pi 5 (margin = `META` status change − partitions appearing; negative means `META` was evaluated
first):

| node | boot | card init | partitions | `waitForUdevd` done | `META` evaluated | margin | outcome |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| node-02 | 01 | 224 | 3345 | 3492 | 3536 | +191 | `waiting -> ready` |
| node-02 | 02 | 227 | 3145 | 3292 | 3389 | +244 | `waiting -> ready` |
| node-02 | 03 | 223 | 3544 | 3623 | 3670 | +126 | `waiting -> ready` |
| node-02 | 04 | 228 | 3331 | 3532 | 3721 | +390 | `waiting -> ready` |
| node-02 | 05 | 222 | 3507 | 3642 | 3718 | +211 | `waiting -> ready` |
| node-02 | 06 | 229 | 3327 | 3408 | 3528 | +201 | `waiting -> ready` |
| node-02 | 07 | 227 | 3309 | 3433 | 3442 | +133 | `waiting -> ready` |
| node-02 | 08 | 225 | 3620 | 3689 | 3804 | +184 | `waiting -> ready` |
| node-02 | 09 | **417** | 3711 | 3586 | 3603 | **-108** | `waiting -> missing` → maintenance |
| node-02 | 10 | **423** | 3818 | 3570 | 3655 | **-163** | `waiting -> missing` → maintenance |
| node-03 | 01 | 227 | 3260 | 3371 | 3466 | +206 | `waiting -> ready` |
| node-03 | 02 | 226 | 3537 | 3518 | 3657 | +120 | `waiting -> ready` |
| node-03 | 03 | 225 | 3427 | 3502 | 3643 | +216 | `waiting -> ready` |
| node-03 | 04 | 219 | 3512 | 3661 | 3826 | +314 | `waiting -> ready` |
| node-03 | 05 | 225 | 3218 | 3391 | 3435 | +217 | `waiting -> ready` |
| node-03 | 06 | **595** | 3834 | 3450 | 3519 | **-315** | `waiting -> missing` → maintenance |
| node-03 | 07 | 230 | 3336 | 3532 | 3533 | +197 | `waiting -> ready` |
| node-03 | 08 | **281** | 3557 | 3441 | 3539 | **-18** | `waiting -> missing` → maintenance |
| node-03 | 09 | 222 | 3554 | 3713 | 3833 | +279 | `waiting -> ready` |
| node-03 | 10 | 228 | 3182 | 3430 | 3325 | +143 | `waiting -> ready` |

*Card init* is the time from `mmc0: SDHCI controller on 1000fff000.mmc` to `mmc0: new UHS-I speed SDR104 SDXC
card`. On successful boots the volumes go straight from `waiting` to `ready` and never pass through `missing`.

A closest-call success, node-03 boot 02 — partitions appear 19 ms *after* `waitForUdevd` returns and the
boot still succeeds:

```
3306  mmc0: SDHCI controller on 1000fff000.mmc [1000fff000.mmc] using ADMA 64-bit
3518  [talos] task waitForUdevd (2/6): done, 921.441759ms
3532  mmc0: new UHS-I speed SDR104 SDXC card at address 0001
3537   mmcblk0: p1 p2 p3 p4 p5 p6
3657  [talos] volume status  volume=META   phase="waiting -> ready"  location=/dev/mmcblk0p4
3759  [talos] volume status  volume=STATE  phase="waiting -> ready"  location=/dev/mmcblk0p5
3869  [talos] task loadConfig (1/1): starting
```

A closest-call failure, node-03 boot 08 — the node gives up **18 ms** before the partitions appear, and
`META` is reported ready 179 ms after the node has already committed to maintenance mode:

```
3273  mmc0: SDHCI controller on 1000fff000.mmc [1000fff000.mmc] using ADMA 64-bit
3441  [talos] task waitForUdevd (2/6): done, 890.037296ms
3539  [talos] volume status  volume=META   phase="waiting -> missing"
3539  [talos] volume status  volume=STATE  phase="waiting -> missing"
3554  mmc0: new UHS-I speed SDR104 SDXC card at address 0001
3557   mmcblk0: p1 p2 p3 p4 p5 p6
3569  [talos] task loadConfig (1/1): starting
3569  [talos] entering maintenance service
3748  [talos] volume status  volume=META   phase="missing -> ready"  location=/dev/mmcblk0p4
3851  [talos] volume status  volume=STATE  phase="missing -> ready"  location=/dev/mmcblk0p5
```

The widest failure, node-03 boot 06 — card initialisation took 595 ms and the partitions arrived 315 ms
after the volumes were declared missing:

```
3194  mmc0: SDHCI controller on 1000fff000.mmc [1000fff000.mmc] using ADMA 64-bit
3450  [talos] task waitForUdevd (2/6): done, 1.032723388s
3519  [talos] volume status  volume=META   phase="waiting -> missing"
3519  [talos] volume status  volume=STATE  phase="waiting -> missing"
3520  [talos] task loadConfig (1/1): starting
3520  [talos] entering maintenance service
3789  mmc0: new UHS-I speed SDR104 SDXC card at address 0001
3834   mmcblk0: p1 p2 p3 p4 p5 p6
4037  [talos] volume status  volume=META   phase="missing -> ready"  location=/dev/mmcblk0p4
4139  [talos] volume status  volume=STATE  phase="missing -> ready"  location=/dev/mmcblk0p5
```

### Where the jitter comes from

Both sides of the race move:

- **Card initialisation on the Pi 5.** 16 of 20 boots initialised in 219–230 ms. The other four took
  281, 417, 423 and 595 ms — and those four are exactly the four failures. Slow card initialisation is the
  dominant cause here, but node-03 boot 08 (281 ms, 18 ms short) shows that it does not take a large outlier
  to lose.
- **The Talos side.** `waitForUdevd` took 848–1266 ms on the Pi 5 and returned 3292–3713 ms after kernel
  start. The missing-decision followed it by 17–98 ms.

`mmc0: cannot verify signal voltage switch` was logged on all 20 Pi 5 boots, successes and failures alike,
so it does not explain the slow initialisations.

### Analysis

**`waitForUdevd` completing does not imply block devices are enumerated.**

`waitForUdevd` returns when udevd's health check passes. At that instant udev has loaded the SDHCI module
chain and the controller has registered, but card enumeration may still be in flight. On every failing boot
the volumes were declared missing 17–98 ms after `waitForUdevd` returned, and nothing in between waits for
mmc: the sequencer in `release-1.14` has only `WaitForUdevd`, `WaitForUSB` and `WaitForCARoots`, and
`waitForUSB` completes in microseconds on these boards (no USB storage present).

**Why the Pi 4 did not fail.** The Pi 4 depends on the same `CONFIG_MMC_SDHCI` module, but on this hardware
the ordering is very different. Its `waitForUdevd` takes 2327–3389 ms (vs 848–1266 ms on the Pi 5), and the
partitions appeared 910–1276 ms *before* it returned, with `META` evaluated ready 178–282 ms after the
partitions, consistently. So the Pi 4 wins the race by roughly a second every time. That comes from its
timing, not from a wait that covers mmc, so I would not assume it is safe on slower cards or under load.

**Possible contributing factor: `CONFIG_MMC_SDHCI` moved from built-in to module in v1.14.**

Diff of `kernel/build/config-arm64` between `release-1.13` and `release-1.14`:

```
CONFIG_MMC_SDHCI          y → m
```

Everything else MMC-related is unchanged (`CONFIG_MMC_SDHCI_BRCMSTB=m`, `CONFIG_MMC_SDHCI_PLTFM=m`,
`CONFIG_MMC_SDHCI_IPROC=m`, `CONFIG_MMC_BCM2835=y`, `CONFIG_MMC_CQHCI=y` in both). With the SDHCI core
built-in, only `sdhci-brcmstb` (+ `sdhci-pltfm`) had to be loaded by udev; now the core itself must be
loaded first, which pushes controller registration later.

I want to be explicit that I have **not** proven causation here — I have not bisected the config. The
defect that matters is the missing wait; this change plausibly moves card enumeration late enough to
expose it, but the race would exist either way.

**Caveat on "it worked before":** the Pi 5 boards previously ran a third-party build
(`johnlaur/talos-builder`, Raspberry Pi vendor kernel) rather than stock v1.13.x, because of the
unrelated macb/RP1 issue (sbc-raspberrypi#91). So this is not a clean stock-1.13-vs-stock-1.14 A/B on
identical hardware, and I cannot assert that stock v1.13.x boots reliably from SD on a Pi 5.

### Reproduction

1. Install Talos v1.14.0 on a Raspberry Pi 5 with the `rpi_5` overlay, system disk on the SD card.
2. Reboot repeatedly (`talosctl reboot --mode powercycle`). About one boot in five entered maintenance mode
   here; runs of five or more successful boots in a row were common.
3. On a failing boot, `talosctl get discoveredvolumes --insecure` shows `mmcblk0p4`/`p5`/`p6`
   (`META`/`STATE`/`EPHEMERAL`) present and intact.
4. `talosctl dmesg --insecure` shows `META`/`STATE` going `waiting -> missing` shortly after `waitForUdevd`
   completes, followed by `mmcblk0: p1 … p6`, followed by `missing -> ready`.
5. `talosctl apply-config --insecure` → node comes up normally on v1.14.0.

Because it is probabilistic, a run of successful boots does not indicate the problem is absent — node-02
booted normally 8 times in a row before failing twice in a row. Expect to reboot 10+ times.

### Suggested fix

Mirror the `usbsettle` approach for mmc: an explicit settle triggered off the presence of an mmc/SDHCI
host controller, waiting for card enumeration to complete (or to be conclusively absent) before the
`meta`/`config` phases run.

More generally, `waitForUdevd` returning on udevd health is not a sufficient barrier for *any* storage
transport whose driver is a module, and the per-transport approach means this shape will keep
reappearing as drivers move to modules. A generic "block device probing has quiesced" barrier before
`reloadMeta`/`loadConfig` would cover mmc, USB, and whatever is next.

### Workaround

`talosctl apply-config --insecure --nodes <ip> --file <config.yaml>` after a failed boot. Not viable
unattended — in particular, any watchdog-triggered reset (`WatchdogTimerConfig`) has roughly a one-in-five
chance of leaving the node in maintenance mode until someone intervenes by hand.
title: v1.14.0: nodes booting from an SD card (SDHCI/mmc) intermittently land in maintenance mode — no settle covers mmc

body:
## Bug Report

### Description
If only a single NTP server is configured (e.g. edge device behind firewall) and the server sends a Kiss of Death packet, the request gets retried every 1s.
Depending on the received KoD code, the client should reduce its polling rate on every subsequent KoD answer. https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/html/rfc5905#section-7.4


Probable cause: the following condition does not match if only a single server is configured, as Kiss of Death response is received and discarded:
https://github.com/siderolabs/talos/blob/a1ede48cb950acb44f0b01242d8594277a17cb4f/internal/pkg/ntp/ntp.go#L232-L235

### Logs
```
<IP>: user: warning: [2026-07-09T07:38:48.642427781Z]: [talos] time query error with server "<NTP>" {"component": "controller-runtime", "controller": "time.SyncController", "error": "kiss of death received"}

<IP>: user: warning: [2026-07-09T07:38:49.67605258Z]: [talos] time query error with server "<NTP>" {"component": "controller-runtime", "controller": "time.SyncController", "error": "kiss of death received"}

<IP>: user: warning: [2026-07-09T07:38:50.690089846Z]: [talos] time query error with server "<NTP>" {"component": "controller-runtime", "controller": "time.SyncController", "error": "kiss of death received"}
```

### Environment

- Talos version:
```Server:
	NODE:        <IP>
	Tag:         v1.12.8

	Built:       
	Go version:  go1.25.10
	OS/Arch:     linux/amd64
	Enabled:     RBAC
```
- Kubernetes version: not relevant
- Platform: bare metal x86
title: bug: NTP query loop every 1s if the only configured server sends a KoD packet

author: smira
body:
Follow-up on https://github.com/siderolabs/talos/pull/13211

There is at least one more (besides Longhorn v1) which might be broken by noexec var:  https://www.vcluster.com/docs/vcluster/troubleshoot/noexec-emptydir-volumes

So the proposal is to flip the defaults:

* without any explicit machine config, noexec defaults to false for EPHEMERAL
* instead, for 1.14+ machine configs, we would inject VolumeConfig document with `noexec: true`

Result:

* users upgrading to 1.14 will not be broken
* new clusters 1.14 if using Longhorn/vcluster might need an adjustment of the base machine config
title: make the noexec for EPHEMERAL opt-in (no-op for upgrades)

author: slehlib
body:
## Bug Report

### Description

Kernel 6.18.15-talos (Talos v1.12.5) triggers a UBSAN out-of-bounds warning in the `bnxt_en` driver during NIC initialization (`bnxt_hwrm_func_qcaps`). The warning is present on all bare metal nodes with Broadcom NICs at every boot. On some nodes, this leads to kernel panics under I/O-intensive workloads (Ceph/RADOS), while other nodes remain stable despite the warning.

This issue does **not** occur on kernel 6.18.8-talos (Talos v1.12.3).

**Observed behavior:**
- UBSAN `__ubsan_handle_out_of_bounds` warning in `bnxt_hwrm_func_qcaps` at every boot on all bare metal nodes
- Warning is non-fatal on some nodes (they remain Ready)
- On other nodes, I/O-intensive workloads (16 concurrent 4MB writes via RADOS) trigger a kernel panic
- Always the same nodes crash, while others with identical hardware/firmware remain stable
- Updating NIC firmware via HPE SPP does not resolve the issue
- Rollback to Talos v1.12.3 (kernel 6.18.8-talos) eliminates both the warning and the crashes

**Tested configurations:**
- Before SPP update: warning + crash under I/O load
- After SPP update: same warning + same crash under I/O load
- Rollback to v1.12.3: no warning, no crash

### Logs

**UBSAN stack trace (present on all affected nodes at boot):**

```
Call Trace:
 <TASK>
 dump_stack_lvl+0x5d/0x90
 ubsan_epilogue+0x5/0x2b
 __ubsan_handle_out_of_bounds.cold+0x54/0x59
 bnxt_hwrm_func_qcaps.part.0+0x191b/0x19a0 [bnxt_en]
 bnxt_fw_init_one_p2+0x34/0xdf0 [bnxt_en]
 bnxt_init_one+0x3ac/0x1010 [bnxt_en]
 local_pci_probe+0x42/0xa0
 work_for_cpu_fn+0x1a/0x30
 process_one_work+0x189/0x2f0
 worker_thread+0x19b/0x320
 ? __pfx_worker_thread+0x10/0x10
 kthread+0xe8/0x220
 ? __pfx_kthread+0x10/0x10
 ret_from_fork+0x126/0x170
 ? __pfx_kthread+0x10/0x10
 ret_from_fork_asm+0x1a/0x30
 </TASK>
---[ end trace ]---
```

### Environment

- **Talos version**: v1.12.5 (kernel 6.18.15-talos) — bug present
- **Talos version**: v1.12.3 (kernel 6.18.8-talos) — no bug
- **Kubernetes version**: v1.35.2
- **Platform**: HPE bare metal (DL360/DL365), 252 GiB RAM
- **NICs**: Broadcom (bnxt_en driver), dual-port, bonded (LACP 802.3ad)
- **NIC firmware**: tested both before and after HPE SPP update — no change
- **Cluster**: 3 control-plane VMs + 4 bare metal workers
- **Workload**: Rook-Ceph with 12 OSDs, all daemons in hostNetwork: true
- **CNI**: Cilium v1.19.1

### Additional Notes

- The regression is in the `bnxt_en` driver between kernel 6.18.8 and 6.18.15
- The function `bnxt_hwrm_func_qcaps` accesses an array out of bounds, suggesting a struct or response size mismatch introduced in the newer kernel
- The UBSAN warning alone is non-fatal, but under heavy network I/O it appears to destabilize the driver on some nodes, leading to kernel panics
- 4 bare metal workers with identical hardware, OS, and firmware — 2 crash under load, 2 remain stable. The cause of this inconsistency is unknown
- This is a separate issue from the BPF verifier panic reported in issue #xxxxx (link to previous issue)
title: Kernel 6.18.15-talos (Talos v1.12.5) triggers a UBSAN out-of-bounds

## Feature Request
Have an option in `imager` to attach configuration and extra data for maintenance mode via an additional filesystem added as partition in the .iso (instead of embedding it in the executable) and have talos maintenance mode discover and mount the filesystem. It would be great if that was a supported way to [embed initial configuration](https://github.com/siderolabs/talos/pull/11851).

### Description
We are currently using `imager` to build an .iso per device for bootstrapping that contains device specific configuration (e.g. network settings, `talos.config.oauth.client_id` etc.). The issue with that is that these device-specific settings are part of the measured boot chain resulting in different PCRs (4, 11 and 12) for each .iso. This makes managing and tracking known good PCRs really hard and also makes it impossible to lock out a specific version of our .iso via the secure boot dbx if that ever became necessary. 

From what I read it's possible to do this directly with `xorriso`; I had success adding an extra partition to an existing .iso simply by padding it, appending an `.img` containing some filesystem (I used FAT32) and modifying the partition table accordingly. The resulting .iso was still bootable and the OS was able to find and mount the partition. I used ubuntu for my tests since it's easier to debug this way rather than with talos running in maintenance mode. 

### Example

Imagine this `profile.yaml`

```yaml
arch: amd64
platform: metal
output:
  kind: secureboot-iso
...
extraData:  # new feature to create an extra file system and append that to the .iso/disk image as partition
  content: 
   - source: /early-machineconfig  # initial machine config docs placed into the extra file system
     target: /early-machineconfig
   - source: /foo  # directory that includes extra data
     target: /foo  # where to place the dir in the extra filesystem
  signer:  # (optional) key used to sign the file system contents
     awsKMSKeyID: ...
     awsRegion: ...
```

imager would then:
* create a signature of the content using the `signer` config and add the public key and signature to the image for verification at runtime (e.g. via a virtual system extension)
* create a filesystem from the paths listed in the `content` section and append that to the iso

talos in maintenance mode would then:
* discover the extra partition (e.g. via a partition label) and mount the filesystem
* if the content was signed use the public key and signature to verify the contents
* apply initial machine documents from some well known location in the filesystem
title: Embedding maintenance mode config via data partition in .iso
