author: ci-robbot
body:
Follow-up from #4345, requested by @mudler ([comment](https://github.com/kairos-io/kairos/issues/4345#issuecomment-5392839383)):

> we are inconsistent in Kairos as with Kubernetes, we pull the image and we use the kairos-agent in the target to do the upgrade (which is correct), and that means that the new code will execute during the upgrade. In non-kubernetes instead, we let the kairos-agent installed in the host to drive the upgrade. It would make sense to exec on the kairos-agent inside the image to drive the rest of the upgrade so the code path can be consistent.

## The two paths today

| | Who pulls the image | Whose `kairos-agent` binary runs |
|---|---|---|
| Kubernetes (system-upgrade-controller) | kubelet, as the upgrade pod's image | **the target image's**, via `/usr/sbin/suc-upgrade` |
| Everything else (`kairos-agent upgrade --source ...`, `kairos-agent upgrade-*` timers, AuroraBoot-driven) | the host agent, into a transition image | **the host's** |

The Kubernetes side is the one that is already right, and it gets there almost by accident: the plan runs the target image as the pod image, and the script inside it calls the agent with a local source.

[`kairos-init/pkg/bundled/bundled.go#L86-L91`](https://github.com/kairos-io/kairos/blob/73f1d10c/kairos-init/pkg/bundled/bundled.go#L86-L91)

```bash
    kairos-agent upgrade --recovery --source dir:/
    ...
    kairos-agent upgrade --source dir:/
```

`HOST_DIR` handling exists only so that the *target* agent reads the *host's* config and partitions rather than the container's:

- [`agent/internal/agent/upgrade.go#L61-L76`](https://github.com/kairos-io/kairos/blob/73f1d10c/agent/internal/agent/upgrade.go#L61-L76)
- [`agent/pkg/utils/k8s/k8s.go`](https://github.com/kairos-io/kairos/blob/73f1d10c/agent/pkg/utils/k8s/k8s.go) (`GetHostDirForK8s`)

## Why the asymmetry costs us

On the non-Kubernetes path every artifact written during an upgrade is written by code that shipped with the **old** image. So any change to an on-disk format has to be understood by agents that were released before the change existed. That is a forward-compatibility requirement on already-shipped binaries, which we cannot satisfy in general.

#4345 is exactly this failure. go-ukify v0.5.0 started writing the type-2 `uki` key in `loader/entries/*.conf`. The host agent (v2.24.10) only knew the `efi` key, so role promotion failed with `no efi entry in .conf file`. The target image's agent had the fix ([kairos-agent#1106](https://github.com/kairos-io/kairos-agent/pull/1106)) already in it, sitting on disk, unused. The two workarounds we gave the reporter were "supply a newer agent" and "rewrite the `.conf` at build time", which are both ways of saying "please make the new code run".

Same class of problem for anything else the upgrade writes: GRUB entries, boot-assessment flags, `.conf` keys, the artifact naming in #2274.

## Proposal

After the image is deployed and mounted, hand the rest of the upgrade to the agent from inside it.

The mechanism is already in the tree. `DeployImage` leaves the target rootfs mounted at `upgradeImg.MountPoint`, and we already chroot into it for the SELinux relabel:

- [`agent/pkg/action/upgrade.go#L148`](https://github.com/kairos-io/kairos/blob/73f1d10c/agent/pkg/action/upgrade.go#L148) `e.DeployImage(&upgradeImg, ...)`
- [`agent/pkg/action/upgrade.go#L171-L174`](https://github.com/kairos-io/kairos/blob/73f1d10c/agent/pkg/action/upgrade.go#L171-L174) `utils.ChrootedCallback(...)`

So the split would be:

1. **Host agent (unavoidably old):** read config, detect partitions, pull and deploy the image. Keep this as small and as format-agnostic as we can, since it can never be updated retroactively.
2. **Target agent (new):** everything that writes a format the new image owns. Rebrand / default GRUB entry, UKI role rotation and `.conf` rewriting, boot-assessment reset, `after-upgrade-chroot` and `after-upgrade` hooks.

That makes the Kubernetes path stop being a special case: it is just the same handoff with step 1 done by kubelet.

## Open questions

- **Handoff contract.** The host agent has to invoke something in the target that old *and* new agents can be asked for. A dedicated subcommand (`kairos-agent upgrade-finalize --state-dir ... --host-dir ...`) is explicit but only exists going forward, so the host needs a "subcommand absent, do it myself" fallback for a while. Downgrades (new host, old target) hit that fallback permanently.
- **UKI.** [`agent/pkg/uki/upgrade.go#L69-L74`](https://github.com/kairos-io/kairos/blob/73f1d10c/agent/pkg/uki/upgrade.go#L69-L74) dumps the source straight into `/efi`. If the upgrade source is an artifact-only trusted-boot image, there is no agent binary in it to exec, and the agent inside the UKI is not reachable without unpacking the `.efi`. This is the case #4345 actually hit, so it needs an answer, not a TODO. Options: require the trusted-boot artifact set to carry the agent binary, or keep a documented ceiling on what the old host agent is expected to parse.
- **Recovery upgrades** deploy to the recovery image; same handoff should apply, but the recovery path does not mount persistent.
- **Failure semantics.** If the target agent exits non-zero mid-finalize, the host agent still owns rollback. Needs to stay a single cleanup stack, not two.

## Acceptance criteria

- One code path, exercised the same way with and without Kubernetes.
- A format change in `loader/entries/*.conf` or the GRUB entries needs no change in any released agent for an upgrade *to* that image to work.
- `suc-upgrade` becomes a thin wrapper, or goes away.
- An upgrade test that installs image A and upgrades to image B where B writes a key A's agent does not know, and passes.

Reported-by follow-up for @Dr-N00B, who hit the concrete instance in #4345.
title: Upgrades should always run the target image's kairos-agent, as the Kubernetes path already does

author: kirankn8
body:
`kairos-agent bootentry --select registration` fails on systems running systemd 255 (Ubuntu 24.04). The entry `registration` does not exist.

**System info:**
```
kairos-agent v2.27.0
kairos 4.0.3 and kairos-init 0.8.5
systemd 255 (255.4-1ubuntu8.14)
Ubuntu 24.04.4 LTS
```

**What happens:**

```
root@edge:~# kairos-agent bootentry --select registration
2026-04-11T05:32:53Z INF Kairos Agent version=v2.27.0
2026-04-11T05:32:53Z INF Boot Mode boot_mode=active_boot
2026-04-11T05:32:53Z INF Boot in uki mode result=true
2026-04-11T05:32:53Z INF Setting default boot entry to registration
2026-04-11T05:32:53Z ERR entry registration does not exist
```

The actual entries on the system are:
```
root@edge:~# ls /efi/EFI/kairos/
active.efi
passive.efi
recovery_install-mode_stylus.registration.efi
statereset_install-mode_stylus.registration.efi
```

There is no entry named `registration`. The entry that boots into registration mode is `recovery` 

**Impact:**

Our `80_stylus.yaml` cloud-init stages call `kairos-agent bootentry --select registration` in `after-reset` to set the node into registration mode after a reset. This silently fails, leaving the node stuck — it boots back into active with no config and crash-loops.

**Confirmed with older agent:**

On the another system with using kairos-agent v.3.5.9, kairos-init v0.5.28, kairos-agent v2.24.10, the reset flow works correctly — the node enters registration mode.
title: kairos-agent bootentry --select broken on systemd < 257 in kairos 4.0.3 and kairos-init 0.8.5

author: wyvernzora
body:
**Kairos version**

- Kairos v4.1.2
- kairos-agent v2.30.0
- kairos-init v0.15.0
- immucore v0.18.0
- Non-UKI GRUB boot
- Upgrade crossed Ubuntu releases

**Describe the bug**

Kairos includes `/usr/libexec` in the default `PERSISTENT_STATE_PATHS`. Immucore copies this directory into `/usr/local/.state/usr-libexec.bind` and bind-mounts it over the selected slot's own `/usr/libexec`.

The copy uses `rsync -aquAX`. Because `--update` prevents an older source file from replacing a newer destination file, booting a newer active image updates the persisted helpers, but subsequently rolling back to an older passive image does not restore that image's older helpers.

The result is a mixed system: executable code from the newer image under `/usr/libexec` is combined with libraries from the older root filesystem.

In the observed rollback, this made `sudo` unusable:

```text
sudo: /lib/aarch64-linux-gnu/libc.so.6: version `GLIBC_2.42' not found
      (required by /usr/libexec/sudo/libsudo_util.so.0)
```

The newer persisted `libsudo_util.so.0` required a glibc symbol that was not provided by the rolled-back image. The older slot itself was bootable, but normal administrative access was lost because its `/usr/libexec` had been hidden by incompatible persisted content.

**To reproduce**

1. Install and boot a Kairos image based on an older distribution release.
2. Upgrade to an image based on a newer distribution release with a newer glibc and sudo build.
3. Boot the newer active image successfully so its `/usr/libexec` contents are synchronized into persistent state.
4. Boot the older passive image through fallback or manual slot selection.
5. Run `sudo`.

The passive image boots with the persisted `/usr/libexec` from the newer image, and `sudo` fails during dynamic linking.

The persisted directory can be observed at:

```text
/usr/local/.state/usr-libexec.bind
```

**Expected behavior**

An A/B rollback should expose a coherent filesystem from the selected slot. Image-owned executables and shared objects under `/usr/libexec` should come from that slot and remain compatible with its libraries.

`/usr/libexec` should not be persisted across slots by default. If persistence is required for some contents, it should be scoped to the image or slot rather than merged globally.

**Source**

`kairos-init` includes `/usr/libexec` in the default persistent paths:

https://github.com/kairos-io/kairos-init/blob/e090b91ffa93747d34422f795820d82813bfd660/pkg/bundled/cloudconfigs/00_rootfs.yaml#L19-L56

Immucore synchronizes the selected slot into the persistent directory and then bind-mounts that directory over the slot path:

https://github.com/kairos-io/immucore/blob/03ce6004d48d228697e7c76e152f56f163324b08/pkg/op/fs.go#L70-L102

The synchronization uses `rsync -aquAX`, preserving newer destination files during rollback:

https://github.com/kairos-io/immucore/blob/03ce6004d48d228697e7c76e152f56f163324b08/internal/utils/mounts.go#L95-L105

The `--update` behavior was introduced in:

https://github.com/kairos-io/immucore/pull/525

The same default persistence and synchronization behavior remains in current releases.
title: Persisting /usr/libexec across A/B slots breaks rollback ABI compatibility

author: itxaka-agent
body:
Split off from #112.

Implement the OS-level hardening controls from **CIS Distribution Independent Linux v2.0.0 Level 1** inside `kairos-init` so every base image ships pre-hardened, and hardening survives A/B upgrade and `kairos-agent reset`.

## Scope

Level 1 only. Level 2 controls (disable USB storage, restrict rsyslog forwarding, etc.) are explicitly out of scope for this issue.

## Controls to add

Grouped by CIS section. Each item is a kairos-init step or a bundled file.

**1.x — Initial setup**
- [ ] Filesystem module blocklist under `/etc/modprobe.d/cis-blocklist.conf` for `cramfs`, `freevxfs`, `jffs2`, `hfs`, `hfsplus`, `udf`. Check impact on interactive install flow before landing.
- [ ] Warning banner content in `/etc/issue.net` (currently only `/etc/issue` is written).
- [ ] File permissions on `/etc/passwd`, `/etc/shadow`, `/etc/gshadow`, `/etc/group`, `/etc/passwd-`, `/etc/shadow-`, `/etc/gshadow-`, `/etc/group-`.

**1.6 — Mandatory access control**
- [ ] Stop disabling SELinux on RHEL-family images in `kairos-init/pkg/stages/steps_init.go`. Ship it in enforcing mode and add whatever policy work is needed for the install and upgrade flow. This is the largest chunk of work in this issue and may deserve its own follow-up ticket after a spike.

**3.x — Network configuration**
- [ ] `/etc/sysctl.d/99-kairos-cis.conf` shipped in the image, covering: `kernel.randomize_va_space=2`, `net.ipv4.conf.all.rp_filter=1`, `net.ipv4.conf.default.rp_filter=1`, `net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies=1`, `net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_source_route=0`, `net.ipv4.conf.all.accept_redirects=0`, `net.ipv4.conf.all.send_redirects=0`, `net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_ra=0`, `net.ipv6.conf.all.accept_redirects=0`.

**4.x — Logging and auditing**
- [ ] Install `auditd` package on all base images.
- [ ] Ship baseline audit rules under `/etc/audit/rules.d/50-kairos.rules`.
- [ ] Depends on kairos-io/kairos#4629 (immucore audit-log persistence) — audit logs must land on the state partition, not the ephemeral rootfs.

**5.x — Access, authentication and authorization**
- [ ] `pam_pwquality` config in `/etc/security/pwquality.conf`.
- [ ] `pam_faillock` config in the appropriate PAM stack per distro.
- [ ] Password aging defaults in `/etc/login.defs`.
- [ ] Cron and at directory permissions.
- [ ] Extend SSH hardening (already partially there in `agent/internal/agent/hooks/ssh_hardening.go`) to cover remaining CIS 5.2 items.

**6.x — System maintenance**
- [ ] Verify `chrony` or `systemd-timesyncd` is present, enabled, and pointed at a configured source on every base image.

## Non-goals

- CIS Kubernetes controls — tracked separately.
- Level 2 controls.
- Distro-specific benchmarks (Ubuntu 22.04, RHEL 9, SLES 15) — Level 1 Distribution Independent first, then optionally layer distro-specific overrides.

## Definition of done

- Every control above is either implemented or has a written justification for "not applicable" in the docs matrix (tracked separately).
- A CI job runs a Lynis or OpenSCAP scan on a booted image and fails if the score regresses below the baseline captured at merge time.

---

*Filed by [`itxaka-agent`](https://github.com/itxaka-agent) as split of #112. Approved by @itxaka.*
title: kairos-init: implement CIS Distribution Independent Linux L1 controls

author: mauromorales
body:
## Summary

On macOS, `kairos-lab` always bridges the VM to `en0`, and never checks that the interface has a link. When `en0` is down — very common on a Mac that is on Wi-Fi, or on a Mac mini with no cable — the VM boots normally, looks healthy, and silently never gets an IP address. Nothing warns the user.

This is the same failure shape as kairos-io/kairos#4432: the tool quietly does something other than what the user expects.

## Reproduce

On a Mac whose active interface is Wi-Fi (`en1`) with the built-in Ethernet port (`en0`) unplugged:

```sh
kairos-lab start -name my-vm     # network mode defaults to bridged
```

**Expected:** an IP from the LAN, or a clear error saying the chosen bridge interface has no link.

**Actual:** the VM boots, the console works, and there is no IP. `kairos-lab status` reports `network mode: bridged` and `bridge iface: en0` with no indication that `en0` is dead.

## Evidence from a real run

Host interface state — `en0` is the built-in Ethernet, unplugged:

```
en0: flags=8963<UP,BROADCAST,SMART,RUNNING,PROMISC,SIMPLEX,MULTICAST> mtu 1500
     media: autoselect (none)
     status: inactive
```

The only active interface is Wi-Fi, and it holds the default route:

```
en1  status=active  ip=192.168.68.61       (default route via 192.168.68.1)
```

The vmnet bridge is built correctly, which is why nothing appears broken:

```
bridge100: status: active
     member: vmenet0
     member: en0
     Address cache:
         52:54:0:12:34:56 Vlan1 vmenet0
```

That address-cache entry is the guest's MAC. The VM is alive and transmitting. Its DHCP requests reach `bridge100`, get forwarded to `en0`, and stop there because `en0` has no link. No DHCP server ever sees them.

## Cause

`internal/app/app.go`:

```go
func defaultBridgeIface() string {
	if runtime.GOOS == "darwin" {
		return "en0"
	}
	if runtime.GOOS == "linux" {
		return ""
	}
	return ""
}
```

Hardcoded, with no validation. The value flows straight into `-netdev vmnet-bridged,id=net0,ifname=` + `cfg.BridgeIface` in `internal/vm/vm.go`.

## Suggested fix

1. **Validate the bridge interface before launching.** If the chosen interface is not `status: active`, fail with an error that names it and lists the active candidates. A dead bridge is never what the user wanted.
2. **Pick a better default.** Instead of a hardcoded `en0`, default to the interface holding the default route (`route -n get default` on macOS). That is right far more often, on laptops especially.
3. **Warn about Wi-Fi.** If the resolved interface is Wi-Fi, print a one-line caveat: bridging a VM onto a Wi-Fi client interface frequently fails, because the access point rejects frames from a MAC other than the one that associated. Better to say so up front than to let the user debug a missing lease.

A workaround exists today (`-bridge-if en1`, or `-network user` with the built-in `hostfwd` 2222→22), but the user has to know the failure mode first, and the tool gives them nothing to go on.
title: start: bridged networking always uses en0 on macOS and never checks the link is up

author: klaymen47
body:
Hi Team,

as discussed in #4338, this task is about the actual migration off of boringcrypto to Go's native FIPS module.

There are no FIPS-related Go code changes needed whatsoever, it's a drop-in replacement.

The only fully certified Go FIPS module version is **v1.0.0**, hence it should be used.

High-level steps:

**Step 1** - Modify the makefile to account for the new *GOFIPS140* flag to be used and drop the *GOEXPERIMENT=boringcrypto* entirely

**Step 2** - Add a proper verification for whether FIPS support is truly enabled and remove the erroneous goreleaser config (*go version -m*)

**Step 3** - Simplify release-scan.yaml's normalization step since the build will no longer have a custom suffix

Out of scope:
- FIPS support for riscv64 architecture*
- *GODEBUG=fips140=only* (officially not recommended for use)

\* - I am a little torn about this. Up to Kairos Team to decide whether this should be implemented as well.
title: feat: Use Go's native FIPS 140-3 module instead of boringcrypto

author: mudler
body:
This issue tracks the integration of a Key Management Service (KMS) with Cluster API (CAPI) to provide secure onboarding for machines provisioned using CAPI.

The goal is to ensure that all secrets and sensitive data required for machine initialization are securely managed and delivered as part of the provisioning workflow. The integration should also support secure machine revocation.

Context:
- Relates to the CAPI integration epic (#120).
- Should address lifecycle management, distribution, and storage of secrets via KMS.
- Must ensure encryption of sensitive data at rest and in transit.
- Documentation and usage examples for operators should be provided.

Expected outcomes:
- Machines initialized via CAPI can securely retrieve needed secrets from KMS.
- The onboarding flow prevents unauthorized access to sensitive information.
- The solution is validated with end-to-end testing and operator guidance.
title: feat: Integrate KMS with CAPI for secure onboarding

author: ci-robbot
body:
## The bug

12.5% of `PR_multiarch` runs (5 of the last 40) lose a job to `Install Go`,
before a single test executes. It is not the toolchain download. It is
`actions/setup-go` restoring its dependency cache and running out the step's
`timeout-minutes: 5`.

The signature is unmistakable: the step burns exactly 5m00s, every time.

| run | job | Install Go |
| --- | --- | --- |
| [34314852826](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/actions/runs/34314852826) | reset tests (FIPS) | 07:45:20 -> 07:50:20 |
| [34294143535](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/actions/runs/34294143535) | reset tests (FIPS) | 5m00s |
| [34162208109](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/actions/runs/34162208109) | acceptance tests | 22:41:42 -> 22:46:42 |
| [34141532218](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/actions/runs/34141532218) | acceptance tests (FIPS) | 17:35:55 -> 17:40:55 |
| [33888029300](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/actions/runs/33888029300) | reset tests (FIPS) | 16:44:38 -> 16:49:38 |

On run 34314852826 the cache restore was at 87.8% of 305 MB when the cap
fired, moving at 0.9 MB/s. At that rate the restore needs about 5m40s, so it
loses to a 5 minute cap by a whisker. Nine jobs in the workflow use
`setup-go`, and any of them can draw the short straw.

Because these are `needs:`-ed test jobs, one timeout turns the whole run red
on a PR whose diff has nothing to do with it. That is what happened twice in
a row on kairos-io/hadron#592.

## The fix

kairos-io/hadron#593 raises the cap on all six active `setup-go` steps from 5
to 15 minutes. `timeout-minutes` only ever aborts a step, so this costs a
healthy run nothing: when the runner network is fine the same step finishes
in seconds and never approaches either number. It only stops a slow-but-
working restore from being killed.

## The part I am deliberately leaving alone

The deeper question is whether a 305 MB cache earns its keep here at all.
`tests/go.mod` is a small Ginkgo suite, 95 modules in `go.sum`, so the bulk
of that 305 MB is `~/.cache/go-build`, not the module set. The cache is a
clear win when the network is healthy and actively worse than no cache when
it is not.

Caching only `~/go/pkg/mod` and dropping the build cache would cut the
restore to a fraction of the size, at the cost of recompiling the test binary
in every job. That is a performance trade I cannot measure from here, and it
wants someone who can benchmark a full run on the ARC runners. Same shape as
#4559. Happy to open that PR if someone picks a direction.
title: hadron CI: setup-go cache restore times out and reddens 12.5% of PR_multiarch runs

author: ci-robbot
body:
Found while tracing the shim/gnu-efi build race in
[kairos-io/hadron#592](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/pull/592).
Filing it separately because the fix is a behaviour change that wants a
maintainer decision, not a drive-by.

## The bug

`Dockerfile.tmpl` declares the load cap once, before the first `FROM`:

```dockerfile
ARG JOBS=16
## Maximum load for make -l
ARG MAX_LOAD=32
```

and then uses it in 150 places:

```dockerfile
RUN make -s -j${JOBS} -l${MAX_LOAD} DESTDIR=/sysroot install
```

A global `ARG` is only a default. A stage has to re-declare `ARG <name>` to
bring it into scope. `JOBS` is re-declared in 113 stages. `MAX_LOAD` is
re-declared in none, so it expands to the empty string everywhere and every
one of those 150 commands runs as:

```
make -s -j16 -l ...
```

GNU make documents bare `-l` as *removing* a previous load limit, so the cap
has never been in effect.

## Evidence

buildkit prints each step with the args that are in scope substituted. From
[run 34233932920](https://github.com/kairos-io/hadron/actions/runs/34233932920),
the shim stage:

```
#915 [shim  9/10] RUN if [ "x86-64" != "riscv64" ]; then     make -s -j16 -l${MAX_LOAD} EFIDIR=hadron ARCH=x86_64 DESTDIR=/tmp/shim install;     fi
```

`ARCH` and `JOBS` are resolved to `x86-64` and `16`. `${MAX_LOAD}` is still
literal, because the shim stage declares `ARG JOBS` and no `ARG MAX_LOAD`.

## Why it needs a decision, not just a patch

The fix is small: add `ARG MAX_LOAD` next to each `ARG JOBS`, or set
`ENV MAX_LOAD` in `stage0` and `stage1` and let the descendants inherit it.
Neither leaks into the shipped image, since the final stages are `FROM
scratch`.

The consequence is not small. buildkit already runs many stages
concurrently, each with `-j16`. Turning the cap on for the first time would
throttle the whole build on the ARC runners, and I have no way to measure
whether 32 is the right number or whether the build gets slower. That is a
call for someone who can benchmark it.

Three options, in the order I would rank them:

1. Put `MAX_LOAD` in scope at 32 and measure a full build against a
   baseline.
2. Put it in scope with a value chosen from the runner size.
3. Drop `-l${MAX_LOAD}` and the `ARG` entirely and say the build is
   deliberately uncapped.

Any of the three is better than the current state, where the Dockerfile
reads as if a cap is set and it is not.

I am happy to open the PR for whichever you pick.
title: hadron: the make load cap has never worked, MAX_LOAD is out of scope in every stage

author: ebourgeois
body:
## Summary

Today, partition encryption in Kairos happens in exactly one place: the `Finish` post-install hook in kairos-agent. If a node is not encrypted at install time, there is no supported way to encrypt it afterwards. Reset reformats persistent as plaintext, and the agent exposes no `kcrypt encrypt` subcommand.

This issue proposes a boot-time step in immucore that encrypts partitions which are *configured* to be encrypted but are not yet LUKS, before they are mounted, using the existing `kcrypt.GetEncryptor()` path. It is the same operation the install hook performs, moved to the first boot of the machine that will actually own the data.

The result: a Kairos image can be installed once, captured as a template or raw image with **no TPM and no key material in it**, and every clone or instance encrypts itself against its own TPM on first boot.

## Use case

Bare-metal-style install on every VM is the bottleneck in our vSphere deployment pipeline. What we want instead:

1. Boot a VM from the Kairos ISO, `kairos-agent install`, power off. **No vTPM attached, no encryption.**
2. Mark that VM as a vSphere template (a "golden" VM).
3. For each new node: clone the template, resize CPU/mem/disk as needed, attach a **fresh vTPM**, inject node-specific cloud-config (static IP, hostname; DHCP is not available to us), power on.
4. On first boot, Kairos notices `COS_PERSISTENT` is configured for encryption but is plaintext, encrypts it against the clone's own TPM, unlocks it, and continues booting normally.

This cuts our node provisioning time roughly in half by removing the install step from the per-node path. The same shape applies to any cloud provider that boots from a prepared disk image (AWS AMI, GCP image, Azure managed image), where today no encryption is possible at all because there is no install step in which the hook could run.

## Why boot-time, and why it is a stronger model than install-time

The core argument is about **where the trust root is created**. Encrypting at boot pushes the trust root back to the first boot of the node that owns the data, which is the only point at which a per-node TPM exists.

**Nothing secret is baked into the template.** The template is a pure function of the OCI image plus a non-secret policy ("encrypt COS_PERSISTENT, use local TPM / use challenger at URL X"). It is reproducible, auditable, and safe to copy, snapshot, export, and store in a content library. There is no LUKS header, no passphrase, no TPM-sealed blob, no NV index contents anywhere in it. Contrast this with encrypting in the template: a vTPM attached to the template and then cloned means every clone shares the same TPM state and the same effective disk key, which VMware explicitly recommends against, and which defeats the point of per-node TPM binding.

**Each node's TPM identity is born on that node.** The vTPM is attached at clone time, so its endorsement key, the RSA keys kcrypt generates, and (in challenger mode) the TPM hash registered with the KMS are all unique to that instance from the moment they exist. Nothing has to be rotated or re-sealed. Downstream node identity systems that attest via TPM (we run SPIRE TPM attestation) get a clean, per-node root.

**Encryption happens before the data exists.** At the point the step runs, persistent has never been mounted on this node. There is no window in which node data is written to plaintext storage and then migrated. The install-time model has the same property, but only if you install on every node; boot-time gives it to templates and raw images too.

**Failure is fail-closed.** If the configuration says "encrypt" and encryption cannot be performed (no TPM present, KMS unreachable), the correct behaviour is to halt the boot with an actionable message, not to continue on plaintext. This is the same semantics `kairos.ram.create_partitions` already ships with: "There is no plaintext fallback: if encryption fails, the boot halts."

**It matches what immucore already does in one flow.** The in-RAM boot path (`EnsurePartitionsDagStep`) already creates *and encrypts* COS_OEM and COS_PERSISTENT inside the initramfs via `kcrypt.GetEncryptor().Encrypt(...)`. This proposal is the natural generalisation: encrypt a partition that exists but is pending, rather than only one that was just created.

## Why the alternatives fall short

| Alternative | Problem |
|---|---|
| Install Kairos on every VM | Works, but is the slow path we are trying to remove. |
| Attach vTPM to the template and encrypt at install | Cloned vTPM state, shared keys across every node. Against VMware guidance and against the purpose of TPM binding. |
| Clone, add vTPM, then `kairos-agent reset` | Reset has no encrypt hook today (`FinishReset` is `CopyLogs` + `Lifecycle`; `FormatPersistent` produces plaintext). Even with a hook added, it costs an extra reboot into recovery per node. Still a useful fallback path, see Phase 3. |
| Encrypt from a cloud-config `boot` stage in bash | By the time cloud-init `boot` runs, immucore has already mounted `/usr/local`. You would be unmounting a live persistent partition and re-implementing kairos-sdk kcrypt internals (NV index layout, PCR policy, challenger protocol) in shell. Brittle and version-coupled. |
| Raw images for cloud providers | Confirms the gap rather than solving it: raw images have no install step, so encryption is currently impossible there. |

## Current state of the code (as of `main`, September 2026)

**kairos-agent**

- `internal/agent/hooks/encrypt.go`: `Encrypt(c)` determines partitions from `c.Install.Encrypt` (or OEM+PERSISTENT under UKI), gets the encryptor via `kcrypt.GetEncryptor`, unmounts, encrypts, unlocks, restores OEM if it was in the list.
- `internal/agent/hooks/hook.go`: `Encrypt` is reached only through `Finish`, which sits in `PostInstall`. `FinishReset`, `FinishUpgrade`, `FirstBoot` do not call it.
- `main.go`: the `kcrypt` command group is `checknv`, `readnv`, `cleanupnv`, `unlock-all`. There is no `encrypt`.
- `pkg/action/reset.go`: `FormatPersistent` unmounts and reformats persistent, plaintext.

**immucore**

- `pkg/dag/dag_normal_boot.go`: order is `MountRoot` → `LvmActivate` → `KcryptUpgrade` → (`MountOEM` ↔ `KcryptUnlock`, order depends on whether OEM is encrypted) → `RootfsStage` → layout, overlays, custom mounts, fstab, `InitramfsStage`.
- `pkg/state/steps.go`: `RunKcrypt` calls `kcrypt.UnlockAllEncryptedPartitions`; `RunKcryptUpgrade` is an existing precedent for a one-shot, idempotent, boot-time transformation of LUKS partitions.
- `pkg/state/steps_ensure_partitions.go`: `EnsurePartitionsDagStep` + `encryptPartitionFn` already encrypt at boot in the in-RAM flow using `kcrypt.GetEncryptor(...).Encrypt([]string{label})`.

So the encryption primitive we need is already in kairos-sdk and already called from immucore. What is missing is the DAG step and the gating logic.

## Proposal

### Configuration

Reuse the existing policy key for *what* to encrypt, and add an explicit opt-in for *when*, because encrypting a plaintext partition is destructive and must never be a surprise on an existing install:

```yaml
install:
  encrypted_partitions:
    - COS_PERSISTENT

kcrypt:
  encrypt_on_boot: true        # new, default false
  # challenger:                # unchanged; local TPM is used when absent
  #   challenger_server: https://kms.example.internal
```

Both live in COS_OEM, which is written at template install time. They are policy, not secrets, so they are safe to bake into the template. Node-specific cloud-config (IP, hostname) continues to arrive through the normal datasources later in boot and is unaffected.

For raw cloud images where OEM cannot be pre-populated, a kernel cmdline token (`kairos.kcrypt.encrypt_on_boot`) mirroring how `kairos.ram.create_partitions` is driven would cover the same need. That can be a follow-up.

### New immucore DAG step: `OpEncryptPending`

Placed in `dag_normal_boot.go` (and `dag_uki_boot.go`) with `WithDeps(OpMountOEM)` when OEM is unencrypted (config must be readable from `/run/cos/oem`), and `OpKcryptUnlock` gains a dependency on it. Behaviour:

1. Read config. If `kcrypt.encrypt_on_boot` is not true → no-op, return.
2. For each label in `install.encrypted_partitions`: locate the partition (`ghw`, same as `UpgradeKcryptPartitions`). If the filesystem is already `crypto_LUKS` → skip. If the label is not found → error.
3. Collect the pending labels. If none → no-op (this is the steady state on every boot after the first).
4. Set `PATH` under UKI (same as `EnsurePartitionsDagStep`).
5. `encryptor := kcrypt.GetEncryptor(log)`; `encryptor.Encrypt(pending)`. Partitions are not mounted at this point in the DAG, so no unmount dance is needed.
6. On error: `HaltWithBanner` with the labels, encryptor name, and the reason (no TPM device, KMS unreachable, etc.). No plaintext fallback.
7. On success, log the labels and return. The existing `OpKcryptUnlock` step then unlocks them exactly as it would on any encrypted node.

Idempotent by construction: step 2/3 makes every subsequent boot a no-op.

### Destructive-write guard

The step luksFormats a partition that has a filesystem on it. Two guards, both cheap:

- The explicit `encrypt_on_boot: true` opt-in (above). Existing nodes that have `install.encrypted_partitions` set were encrypted at install and are already LUKS, so they hit the skip branch regardless; the opt-in is belt-and-braces for anyone who set the policy but whose install failed silently.
- Documented clearly: enabling `encrypt_on_boot` on a node that already has plaintext data in the listed partitions destroys that data. In the template flow this is exactly what is wanted (template persistent contains nothing worth keeping), but it needs to be in the docs in bold.

### `kairos-agent` changes (small, optional but recommended)

- `kairos-agent kcrypt encrypt <label>...`: a thin CLI wrapper over the same sdk call, for operators who want to do this manually from recovery. Also makes the e2e test trivially scriptable.
- Add the same "encrypt pending partitions" call to the reset path after `FormatPersistent` (William's suggestion from Slack). Gives a second, reboot-based route to the same end state and makes reset consistent with install.

### Testing

- New e2e in kairos: install in QEMU **without** swtpm, poweroff, attach swtpm, boot with `encrypt_on_boot: true`. Assert `kairos-agent state` lists COS_PERSISTENT as encrypted, `/usr/local` is mounted from a dm-crypt device, and a second reboot is a clean no-op.
- Negative test: same flow, no TPM attached, assert boot halts with the banner and persistent remains untouched (still plaintext, no partial LUKS header).
- Challenger variant using the existing challenger e2e harness.

### Documentation

- New section in `docs/advanced/partition_encryption`: "Encrypting on first boot (templates and cloud images)", with the vSphere template flow as the worked example and the destructive-write warning.

## Path forward / phases

1. **Phase 1, immucore:** `OpEncryptPending` step, config gating, halt semantics, unit tests with `encryptPartitionFn` stubbed (same pattern as the in-RAM tests). This alone unblocks the vSphere template use case.
2. **Phase 2, kairos:** e2e tests above, docs.
3. **Phase 3, kairos-agent:** `kcrypt encrypt` subcommand and reset-path encryption for parity.
4. **Phase 4, cloud images:** kernel cmdline opt-in for raw images where OEM cannot carry the policy; validate on at least one public cloud.

I am happy to take Phase 1 and open the PR against immucore, and to follow with Phases 2 and 3. Would appreciate a maintainer sanity check on: the config key name and location (`kcrypt.encrypt_on_boot` vs something under `install`), whether the step should also cover UKI in the first cut, and whether you want the destructive-write guard to be stricter than an opt-in flag (for example, refusing if the target filesystem is non-empty).

## Context

Slack thread in `#kairos` (CNCF), September 2026. Related: `kairos.ram.create_partitions` (netboot docs) already encrypts at boot in initramfs and is the direct precedent for this proposal.
title: feat: Boot-time encryption of pending partitions: encrypt COS_PERSISTENT on first boot, not at install

author: mauro-agent
body:
## The problem

`reusable-qemu-test.yaml` pushes its bundles test image to a **fixed tag**:

```yaml
      - name: Build and push bundle image
        with:
          push: true
          tags: quay.io/kairos/ci-temp-images:bundles-test
```

No PR number, no commit SHA, no matrix dimension. Every run of the `bundles` test in every pull request writes the same tag.

## Why it matters

Two pull requests running the `bundles` test concurrently overwrite each other's image, and either may pull the other's. The test then validates a bundle built from **someone else's branch** while reporting against yours.

The failure mode is nasty because it is silent and intermittent: no error, no warning, just an occasional green that means nothing or a red that has nothing to do with the change under review. It looks exactly like flake, so it gets retried rather than investigated.

Every other image on this path is already disambiguated — the factory tags with `$FLAVOR-$FLAVOR_RELEASE-$VARIANT-$ARCH-$MODEL-$COMMIT_SHA`. This one is the exception.

## Suggested fix

Include the run's identity in the tag, in keeping with the surrounding convention. Any of:

```yaml
tags: quay.io/kairos/ci-temp-images:bundles-test-${{ github.event.pull_request.number }}
tags: quay.io/kairos/ci-temp-images:bundles-test-${{ github.sha }}
tags: quay.io/kairos/ci-temp-images:bundles-test-${{ github.run_id }}
```

The SHA form matches what the factory already does. Whichever is chosen, the consuming step in the same job needs the same reference.

Worth pairing with a `quay.expires-after` label so the extra tags do not accumulate — `image-pr.yaml` already applies `quay.expires-after=6h` to its images, and this one currently carries none.

## Not a security issue

Both writer and reader are authenticated pushes to a repository only the org can write to, so this is not a poisoning vector. It is a correctness and debuggability problem.

Found while reviewing [#4309](https://github.com/kairos-io/kairos/pull/4309).

---

<sub>🤖 Filed by `mauro-agent`, an AI agent operated by @mauromorales, with his review.</sub>
title: CI: bundles test pushes to a fixed tag, so concurrent PRs overwrite each other

author: ci-robbot
body:
🤖 Filed by `ci-robbot`, an automated agent operated by @mudler. Found by
static analysis while evaluating gohawk for #4606, then confirmed by reading
the code. Not a report from a user-visible failure.

**Kairos version:** `master` @ `c50626fb`

**Describe the bug**

Two defects in `Elemental.PartitionAndFormatDevice`
(`agent/pkg/elemental/elemental.go:66-113`).

### 1. The install target's file descriptor leaks on every failure path

`partitioner.NewDisk` calls `diskfs.Open(device)`, so the returned `*Disk`
owns an open fd on the install target. It is closed exactly once, on the happy
path:

https://github.com/kairos-io/kairos/blob/c50626fb/agent/pkg/elemental/elemental.go#L109

Three `return err` sit between the open and that `Close`:
`disk.NewPartitionTable`, `disk.ReReadPartitionTable` and
`disk.GetPartitionTable`. Each returns with the fd still open.

This is not just tidiness. A held fd on a block device is one of the things
that makes the kernel refuse to re-read its partition table, which is the
operation the surrounding code already retries five times. So a first failure
can make a subsequent attempt in the same process fail for a reason that did
not exist before.

### 2. The `ReReadPartitionTable` retry loop's result is discarded

The loop breaks on success, and is then followed by an *unconditional* sixth
`disk.ReReadPartitionTable()` whose error is the one actually checked. A
transient failure on that extra call throws away whatever the five retries
achieved. Two smaller things in the same block: `time.Sleep(time.Duration(i) *
time.Second)` sleeps 0s after the first failure, and the log line says
"Waiting 5 seconds" while the code waits `i`.

@itxaka-agent documented both in a `NOTE:` in #4549 and deliberately left them
(that PR is a pure refactor to a shared retry helper). No tracking issue
existed, hence this one.

**Expected behavior**

`disk` is released on every return path, and the retry loop's outcome is the
one that decides whether the function fails.

**Additional context**

Fixing 1 is not a bare `defer disk.Close()`: the existing happy-path call logs
the close error rather than returning it, so a defer has to either replace that
call or guard against a double close.

Reproduce the detection:

```
go install github.com/kojah/gohawk@v0.3.0
mkdir -p kairos-init/pkg/bundled/binaries/fips   # embed stubs
CGO_ENABLED=0 gohawk ./agent/pkg/elemental/
```

```
warning[resourcelifetime]: owned resource from partitioner.NewDisk is not released on every return path
  --> agent/pkg/elemental/elemental.go:72:15
```

`golangci-lint` as configured today does not report this; `bodyclose` would not
either, since it only models `*http.Response`. See #4606.
title: PartitionAndFormatDevice leaks the target disk fd on failure, and discards its own retry loop's result

This card is the epic to track all the issues related to streamlining derivatives creation. This includes all the tools, design document, flows in place in order to get full OS image building easied out and also carried in Kubernetes native contexts, including onboarding.

The ultimate goal is to be able to convert upstream images directly with our CRD and artifacts built from our factory - if someone wants can build them manually or just use ours.

## Design goals
- Be able to create a derivative from a Dockerfile with standard container build tools (buildah, docker, etc.)
- Be able to create a derivative from a Kubernetes manifest CRD, using also artifacts from the Kairos factory in a "static", immutable way. Instead of running dynamic commands, we focus on statically creating high reproducible builds of images.
- Be able to create custom OS from Kairos core releases from the CRD and a dedicated CLI with additional customizations: such as kernel, packages, etc.
- Be able to create assets to boot the OS in different scenarios: raw disk images for cloud, ISOs for baremetal, disk images for embedded platforms, netboot artifacts for booting from network
- Be able to netboot seamlessly from network with zero-touch infrastructure configuration - plugging into the existing network with our CRDs.

Kairos is used to provision the immutable OS on a diverse set of edge devices, where users can have the flexibility to build their own image and add their own drivers etc. for specific edge hardware. Devices can be provisioned and added to k8s clusters in an automated way thanks to kairos.  

### Deployment footprint/scale

Nearly a dozen edge devices and some vm's.

### Why Kairos

Kairos is the most open tool for OS management and immutability. Edge devices can often only run specific types of OS, and with Kairos tooling we can stay close to the OS the device vendor supports.
 
The fact that the OS is handled as an OCI image, gives the added benefit that the OS can be handled just like any other cloud native artifact.
 
Many small edge devices don't have a BMC or even support for PXE booth. With the A/B partition upgrade that kairos provides, we can manage the devices in a similar way nonetheless, without the need for a central component in the network.

Guaranteed reproducibility and OS management in cloud-native (gitops) way of working. It really brings a (mature) cloud-native way of working to a (challenging) edge environment.

author: mauromorales
body:
## Summary

Booting Fedora-based Kairos riscv ISOs under **`qemu-system-riscv64`** on **Linux** (**`-accel tcg`**, **`virt`** machine, UEFI via distro **`ovmf-riscv64`** / **`qemu-uefi-riscv64`**) can fail early in userspace before the live root overlay is set up. The failure goes away when **`immucore` in the live initrd is built without UPX** (e.g. **`kairos-init`** with **`SKIP_UPX`** or equivalent).

## Observed behaviour

- **`immucore`** terminates with **`unhandled signal 11`** (**store/AMO page fault**) while executing from a mapping reported as **`memfd:upx`** (VMA name indicates UPX’s run-time unpacking path).

- Subsequent errors are downstream of **`immucore`** not completing (e.g. **`overlayfs: failed to resolve '/run/rootfsbase'`**, emergency shell).

- Same ISO path **could boot under QEMU via UTM on macOS** in at least one environment, suggesting **different host TCG backend / QEMU build** affects whether the UPX **`memfd` stub** path survives.

## Relevant upstream wiring

In **`kairos-io/kairos-init`**, the **`compress`** target still runs **`upx`** on the standard **`OUTPUT_DIR`** binaries—including **`immucore`**—for **`riscv64`**. UPX on the **`OUTPUT_DIR_FIPS`** set is skipped for **`riscv64`** because FIPS artifacts are not used there—not the primary bundle.

Unless the pipeline sets **`SKIP_UPX`**, **riscv **`immucore`** is UPX-compressed**.

## Sanity check after local changes

After changing **`kairos-init`** to skip UPX, always confirm the ISO you boot actually carries the new initrd:

- Extract **`/boot/initrd`** from the **exact** ISO image and **`file`** / **`strings`** **`immucore`** inside—or check for **`UPX`** signatures. A stale or wrong artifact will still reproduce **`memfd:upx`** even if the Makefile was updated.

## Suggested directions

1. **Document**: riscv QEMU-on-Linux testers may need **`SKIP_UPX=1`** (or unpacked **`immucore`**) until this interaction is characterized.

2. **Consider**: defaulting **`riscv64`** to **no UPX** in **`kairos-init`** **`compress`** (or gating UPX behind an explicit flag) if other platforms behave similarly under TCG.

3. **Upstream triage**: treat as UPX/memfd + **RISC-V TCG** toolchain edge case vs **Kairos** proper once reproduction is nailed down (**QEMU version**, host ISA, **`kairos-agent`** / **`immucore`** version).

## Environment snapshot (representative)

- Guest: Kairos Fedora riscv ISO (Hadron-era build).
- Host: Linux, **`qemu-system-riscv64`**, TCG, UEFI **`ovmf-riscv64`**.
- Confirmation: disabling UPX for **`immucore`** removed the **`memfd:upx`** crash and allowed normal live boot continuation.

## Related

- Parent: kairos-io/kairos#4083
- **PR:** kairos-io/kairos-init#352 — skips UPX for `linux/riscv64` bundled binaries in release Docker + GoReleaser, plumbs `DISABLE_UPX` in the production Dockerfile and Makefile (**addresses this issue’s `immucore` / UPX pathway**); GRUB EFI package-map changes in the same PR are separate work for Fedora/riscv image composition.
title: riscv64: UPX-packed immucore crashes under QEMU TCG on Linux (memfd stub); SKIP_UPX / non-UPX build boots

author: jimmykarily
body:
At initramfs state, there is no DNS setup and it's not possible to resolve domains. Kairos config file may include things like the kcrypt challenger server, which may be served on a specific domain. No DNS means, those services won't be accessible resulting in a system that doesn't boot correctly.

Our documentation mentions some ways to configure DNS (https://kairos.io/docs/reference/configuration/#syntax) but this doesn't seem to work on systemd based systems at least on the initramfs stage.

Users have workarounds like this:

```
stages: 
  boot.before:
     - name: "DNS settings"
       commands:
       - echo "DNS=8.8.8.8 8.8.4.4" >> /etc/systemd/resolved.conf
       - echo -e "\n[DHCP]\nUseDNS=false" >> /etc/systemd/network/20-dhcp.network
       - systemctl restart systemd-networkd
       - systemctl restart systemd-resolved
```
(thanks @christianprim) 


but we should provide a simpler way to configure DNS on any system.
title: No DNS at initramfs stage

author: ci-robbot
body:
## The problem

`AuroraBoot` `main` is red. The `unit-tests` job in run
[34519972825](https://github.com/kairos-io/AuroraBoot/actions/runs/34519972825)
took **1h56m** and then failed on a suite timeout, with one spec responsible:

```
[TIMEDOUT] start-pixie [It] does not fail validation when cloud-config-file is empty
Ran 42 of 42 Specs in 6996.429 seconds
FAIL! - Suite Timeout Elapsed -- 41 Passed | 1 Failed
```

The spec was added by AuroraBoot#803, merged at 18:48 UTC on 2026-09-10.
`Tests` on `main` was green at 10:15 (`60217193`, before it) and red at 19:22
(`63da888`, after it).

## Root cause

The spec bounds the run with a 200ms context:

```go
ctx, cancel := context.WithTimeout(context.Background(), 200*time.Millisecond)
defer cancel()
err = app.RunContext(ctx, []string{"", "start-pixie", "", "rootfs.squashfs", "127.0.0.1", "0", "initrd.img", "vmlinuz"})
```

That context is inert. `ops.StartPixiecore` returns a `func(ctx context.Context) error`
whose body never reads `ctx` ([`pkg/ops/netboot.go:65-80`](https://github.com/kairos-io/AuroraBoot/blob/63da888/pkg/ops/netboot.go#L65-L80)),
and `pkg/netboot.Server` does not take one at all. It ends in
`server.Serve()`, which blocks on `err = <-s.errs` until a fatal error or an
explicit `Shutdown()`. Nothing calls `Shutdown`.

Ginkgo's own progress report names the blocked frame:

```
goroutine 7 [chan receive, 116 minutes]
  github.com/kairos-io/netboot/server.(*Server).Serve(...)  server/server.go:148
  github.com/kairos-io/AuroraBoot/pkg/netboot.Server(...)   pkg/netboot/server.go:53
  ...StartPixiecore.4(...)                                  pkg/ops/netboot.go:80
> internal/cmd/start-pixie.go:90                            return f(c.Context)
> internal/cmd/start-pixie_test.go:43                       err = app.RunContext(ctx, ...)
```

`server.go:148` is the `<-s.errs` receive.

## Why it does not reproduce everywhere

`Serve` binds a raw socket for DHCP snooping plus UDP 69 and 4011, all of which
need privileges. Unprivileged, it returns in ~20ms:

```
returned after 22.218346ms with err=listen ip4:17 0.0.0.0: socket: operation not permitted
```

The CI job runs as root (`/root/go/pkg/mod` in the stack trace above), so all
four listeners come up and `Serve` blocks. The spec therefore passes for anyone
without `CAP_NET_RAW` and hangs on the runner.

## Impact

Every `Tests` run on `main` and on every PR spends two hours in `unit-tests`
before failing, and `main` stays red.

## Fix

Thread the context through `pkg/netboot.Server` and call `Shutdown()` when it is
done. `server.Server.Shutdown()` already exists for exactly this. The CLI path
passes `context.Background()`, so a real netboot session keeps serving.

PR: AuroraBoot#811
title: AuroraBoot unit-tests: start-pixie spec hangs for 2h because StartPixiecore ignores its context

author: ci-robbot
body:
## What is happening

`AuroraBoot`'s `e2e-tests` job loses specs to a failing `docker pull`, and the log never says why.

[Run 34493887894](https://github.com/kairos-io/AuroraBoot/actions/runs/34493887894/job/102927314370) lost three `build-uki` specs at once. This is the entire report for one of them:

```
• [FAILED] [13.177 seconds]
build-uki secure-boot-enroll setting in loader.conf when secure-boot-enroll is not set [BeforeEach]
  STEP: pulling the container image @ 09/10/26 16:44:19.003
  [FAILED] in [BeforeEach] - e2e/build_uki_test.go:65

  [FAILED] Unexpected error:
      <*exec.ExitError | 0x33d3e25320e0>:
      exit status 1
      {
          ProcessState: { pid: 11804, status: 256, rusage: {...} },
          Stderr: nil,
      }
  occurred
```

No registry error, no image name, no rate-limit line. `grep`ping the full 23k-line job log around that timestamp returns nothing further.

## Why

`e2e/suite_test.go`:

```go
func PullImage(image string) (string, error) {
	runCmd := fmt.Sprintf(`docker pull %s`, image)
	return utils.SH(runCmd)
}
```

Two things line up badly:

1. All nine call sites are `_, err := PullImage(image)`, so the returned output is dropped.
2. `utils.SH` uses `CombinedOutput`, which leaves `ExitError.Stderr` nil. Gomega then formats the bare `*exec.ExitError`, whose `Error()` is `"exit status 1"`.

So the only channel carrying docker's message is the one the caller throws away.

## Why it matters now

`e2e-tests` is intermittently red across AuroraBoot PRs (failures at 15:10, 15:24, 19:12, 19:24 and 19:51 on 2026-09-10; successes at 10:20, 11:46, 14:09, 14:14 and 18:12), and the reds are not all the same fault. Some are the loop-device teardown in the ESP tests, some are this. Without the pull output there is no way to tell a rate limit from a network fault from a bad tag, or to say whether this is another face of #4553.

For the record, the tag itself is fine: `quay.io/kairos/fedora:40-core-amd64-generic-v3.3.3-uki` is still active on quay (last modified 2025-03-25), so the image is not missing.

## Fix

Fold the combined output into the error inside `PullImage`, so all nine call sites benefit without being touched. `buildISO` in the same `BeforeEach` already does the equivalent via `Expect(err).ToNot(HaveOccurred(), out)`, so this only closes the one remaining blind spot on that path.

This does not make the pull succeed. It makes the next failure diagnosable.
title: AuroraBoot e2e: a failed docker pull reports only "exit status 1", the output is discarded

author: ci-robbot
body:
Found while QA'ing #4519. It is not in that PR, it is in immucore, and it will
keep any SELinux-enabled install from holding a label on a persistent path.

## What happens

`MountBind`'s prepare callback runs on **every** boot and rsyncs the image path
into the persistent state dir:

- [`immucore/pkg/op/fs.go:96-101`](https://github.com/kairos-io/kairos/blob/master/immucore/pkg/op/fs.go#L96-L101) `CreateIfNotExists(rootMount)`, `CreateIfNotExists(stateDir)`, then `SyncState(rootMount, stateDir)`
- [`immucore/internal/utils/mounts.go:104`](https://github.com/kairos-io/kairos/blob/master/immucore/internal/utils/mounts.go#L104) is `rsync -aquAX <src> <dst>`

`-X` is `--xattrs`, and it makes the destination's xattr set *match* the
source's. That includes **deleting** an attribute the destination has and the
source does not.

When the OS image does not ship the bind-mount path (say `/var/lib/rook` for a
`persistent.bind` entry), `CreateIfNotExists(rootMount)` creates the source
directory itself, in the initramfs, before any policy is loaded. It carries no
`security.selinux` at all. The destination is the real `.bind` state dir, which
does carry one after the first relabel.

So boot 0 relabels and everything is fine, and boot 1 onwards silently strips
the label back off. The `.bind` directory keeps its inode and gets its ctime
bumped by rsync setting attrs, and the files created under it at runtime keep
their labels, because they are not in the source and there is no `--delete`.
That asymmetry is exactly what was reported on #4519.

## Reproduction

Not SELinux-specific, it is rsync's `--xattrs` contract. With a real rsync
(3.5.0), a `user.` attribute standing in for the label:

```
$ mkdir -p src/var-lib-rook dst/var-lib-rook.bind
$ setfattr -n user.selinuxproxy -v 'system_u:object_r:container_var_lib_t:s0' dst/var-lib-rook.bind
$ getfattr -d -m - dst/var-lib-rook.bind
user.selinuxproxy="system_u:object_r:container_var_lib_t:s0"

$ rsync -aquAX src/var-lib-rook/ dst/var-lib-rook.bind/
$ getfattr -d -m - dst/var-lib-rook.bind
(nothing)
```

`-u` does not protect it: `--update` compares mtimes on files, and directory
attributes are applied regardless.

## Scope

Only the roots of the two trees can disagree this way. Anything *below* `src`
comes out of the OS image and was labelled at build time, so `-X` propagates
correct labels downward and should keep doing so. The wipe is confined to the
directory immucore itself created.

Worth noting the agent-side sync went the other way and never grew this
problem: [`agent/pkg/utils/common.go:182-189`](https://github.com/kairos-io/kairos/blob/master/agent/pkg/utils/common.go#L182-L189)
uses `--archive --acls` with no `-X`, above a comment asking this exact
question:

```go
// TODO: copy xattr if possible or needed for selinux contexts? Or do we just relabel those on first boot?
```

The two sync paths disagree today, and only the immucore one can clobber a
label.

## Fix

Keep `-X`, since dropping it would lose legitimate xattrs (capabilities and
labels) that the image does carry, but stop the sync from removing attributes
from the state dir root. A recursive `restorecon` over the persistent tree is
not needed for this.
title: immucore: SyncState strips the SELinux label off persistent bind-mount state dirs on every boot

author: mauromorales
body:
## Summary

`kairos-lab start <path-to-iso>` silently ignores the positional path and boots a different ISO. There is no error and no warning. The user believes they booted the ISO they named, and every conclusion drawn from that VM is wrong.

The ISO path is only accepted through the `-iso` flag. A bare positional argument is parsed and discarded.

## Reproduce

```sh
# One ISO already in the downloads cache, e.g. from a previous `kairos-lab download`
kairos-lab start ~/Downloads/kairos-ubuntu-24.04-core-arm64-generic-v1.0.0.iso
```

**Expected:** the named ISO boots, or the command fails with a usage error.

**Actual:** a completely different ISO boots — the one already in the downloads cache. The command prints nothing about the substitution.

```
Hadron Linux (Fri Feb  6  2026)
Kernel 6.19.2-hadron on an aarch64
[kairos@kairos-ccb2 ~]$ cat /etc/kairos-release
KAIROS_FLAVOR="hadron"
KAIROS_FLAVOR_RELEASE="v0.0.4"
KAIROS_VARIANT="standard"
KAIROS_VERSION="v4.0.3"
KAIROS_INIT_VERSION="v0.8.4"
```

The ISO that was named on the command line is `ubuntu` / `core` / `v1.0.0` / kairos-init `v0.16.2`. I verified its contents directly: `unsquashfs` of `/rootfs.squashfs` inside that ISO gives exactly those values, so the ISO itself was fine.

`~/Library/Application Support/kairos-lab/state.json` records what actually ran:

```
"-cdrom", "…/downloads/kairos-hadron-v0.0.4-standard-arm64-generic-v4.0.3-k3sv1.35.2+k3s1.iso"
```

## Cause

`runStart` in `internal/app/app.go` parses its flag set and never inspects the remaining positional arguments:

```go
func runStart(args []string, stdin io.Reader, stdout, stderr io.Writer, store *state.Store) error {
	fs := flag.NewFlagSet("start", flag.ContinueOnError)
	isoPath := fs.String("iso", "", "path to ISO file")
	…
	if err := fs.Parse(args); err != nil {
		return err
	}
```

`fs.NArg()` is never checked, so the positional path is dropped. `*isoPath` stays empty, and the code falls through to:

```go
res, err := iso.ResolveForStart("", downloadsDir, stdin, stdout)
```

`ResolveForStart` with an empty path calls `SelectDownloaded`, which auto-selects when exactly one ISO is cached (`internal/iso/iso.go`):

```go
if len(isos) == 1 {
	return isos[0], nil
}
```

With one cached ISO there is no prompt at all. The substitution is completely silent. With two or more, the user does at least get a menu — but the menu gives no hint that their argument was thrown away, so it reads as a normal prompt.

The same `fs.NArg()` gap exists in the other subcommands that build a flag set, so a mistyped positional argument is dropped there too.

## Suggested fix

**Reject unknown positional arguments.** After `fs.Parse(args)`, return a usage error when `fs.NArg() > 0`:

```go
if fs.NArg() > 0 {
	return fmt.Errorf("unexpected argument %q: pass the ISO with -iso", fs.Arg(0))
}
```

This turns a silent wrong boot into an immediate, obvious failure, and the error text points at the flag.

**Do not make the positional form work.** That is what `-iso` is for. Accepting both would give the same option two spellings and leave the flag looking optional when it is the interface.

Apply the same check to the other subcommands that build a flag set, so a mistyped positional argument fails there too.

Separately: when `SelectDownloaded` auto-selects the only cached ISO, printing one line that names the chosen ISO would make this class of mistake self-evident. Right now the quiet path is completely silent.

## Impact

This is a correctness trap rather than a crash. The VM boots, the login works, and everything looks normal. The user tests the wrong image and trusts the result. In this case it produced a confident, wrong bug report against AuroraBoot, which had built the correct artifact all along.

---

*Note: this is not an agent acting on its own. Mauro used AI to help investigate this and write it up.*
title: start: positional ISO path is silently ignored and a different ISO boots

author: ci-robbot
body:
## What happens

`Client.GetURL` in `agent/pkg/implementations/http/client.go` builds a `grab.Request` and leaves `NoResume` at its zero value. grab then treats whatever is already at the destination as a partially completed download of the same URL. It never verifies that assumption, and there is no checksum anywhere in this path, so an unrelated leftover file silently steers the result.

`grab/v3@v3.0.1`, `client.go:236` `validateLocal`, gives three outcomes depending on the size of the local file:

| Local file vs remote | grab does | `GetURL` returns | On disk afterwards |
|---|---|---|---|
| shorter | sets `Range: bytes=<localsize>-` and **appends** | `nil` | old prefix + new suffix, a hybrid of two artifacts |
| longer | `ErrBadLength` | `bad content length` | untouched, and every retry fails identically |
| same size | keeps it, `DidResume = true` | `nil` | the stale file, never the remote one |

The first row is the bad one: a corrupt file, reported as a successful download.

## Where it bites

`InstallExtension` (`agent/pkg/action/sysext.go:302`) downloads into `sysextDir`, which is persistent (`/var/lib/kairos/extensions`), under a name derived from the URI:

```go
return h.cfg.Client.GetURL(sdkLogger.NewNullLogger(), h.uri, filepath.Join(s, filepath.Base(h.uri)))
```

So re-installing a sysext from a URL whose artifact has been republished at a larger size writes `old bytes 0..N` + `new bytes N..end` to `/var/lib/kairos/extensions/<name>.raw` and exits 0. systemd-sysext then gets a corrupt image. If the republished artifact is smaller, the install fails with `bad content length` and keeps failing until someone deletes the file by hand, which is not something the error text suggests.

The doc comment on `InstallExtension` says "It will check if the extension is already installed before doing anything". It does not, and this is what happens instead.

The other two callers are `GetSource` (`agent/pkg/utils/common.go:427`), used for install and upgrade sources, and `installCatalogExtension` (`agent/pkg/cmd/root.go:1586`). The catalog one is safe by accident: it downloads to a `UnixNano`-suffixed temp path, so the destination never pre-exists.

## Why it is a bug and not a feature

The other two `Download` implementations in the same interface overwrite. `fileSource.Download` opens with `os.O_CREATE|os.O_WRONLY|os.O_TRUNC` (`sysext.go:470`) and `dockerSource.Download` extracts over the target. Only the HTTP one resumes, so `sysext install file://...` and `sysext install oci://...` are idempotent while `sysext install https://...` is not.

Resume is only safe when you can prove the local bytes belong to the same artifact. Nothing here does: no checksum, no ETag, no If-Range.

## Reproduction

Local, no network, four specs in `agent/pkg/implementations/http`. Against master the shorter-file case produces:

```
Expected
    <string>: OLD-CONTENT-THAT-IS-LONGER-THAN-THE-OLD-ONE
to equal
    <string>: NEW-CONTENT-THAT-IS-LONGER-THAN-THE-OLD-ONE
```

The first 11 bytes are the stale file, the rest is the remote body, and `GetURL` returned `nil`.

## Fix

Set `req.NoResume = true`. That covers all three rows above. The cost is that a genuinely interrupted large download restarts instead of resuming, which is the right trade while nothing validates the resumed bytes.

Filed with a PR.

🤖 Filed by `ci-robbot`, an automated agent operated by @mudler.
title: kairos-agent: GetURL resumes onto an unrelated existing file, silently corrupting a re-downloaded sysext

body:
https://spectrocloud.slack.com/archives/C056VJ4V1HP/p1755285335046689

We propose adding a dry-run command to `kairos-init` to display the stages and steps that would execute without making any changes to the system. This would help users debug configurations, verify workflows, or understand the initialization process before applying it.

**Problem**
Currently, `kairos-init` executes stages immediately without an option to preview the actions. This limits transparency and makes it harder to validate configurations.

**Proposed Solution**
Add a `--dry-run` flag to `kairos-init` that: 
1. Parses the configuration and identifies all stages to be executed. 
2. Outputs a detailed list of steps (e.g., package installations, file modifications, service configurations) without applying them. 
3. Includes stage dependencies and order of execution. 

**Acceptance Criteria**
- [ ] Implement `--dry-run` flag in `kairos-init` to show execution steps. 
- [ ] Document the flag in the CLI help and README. 
- [ ] Provide examples in the documentation (e.g., `kairos-init --dry-run config.yaml`). 
- [ ] Ensure the output is machine-readable (e.g., JSON format) for automation. 
- [ ] Validate that no system changes occur during a dry run.

**Use Cases**

- Educating users about the initialization process.

**Additional Notes**
This feature aligns with Kairos' focus on transparency and reproducibility. It would complement existing tools like `kairos-bundle` and `kairos-image` by providing a safety check before deployment.

author: ci-robbot
body:
## Two problems, one root cause

### 1. No CI job ever builds a k0s image

`pr.yaml` and `master.yaml` build six `build-iso` cells between them. Every one is either `kubernetes_distro: ''` or `kubernetes_distro: 'k3s'`. The only place a k0s image is ever produced is `release.yaml`'s `build-iso-k0s` job, which runs when a tag is pushed.

That matters because the k0s provider does real work at **image build time**, not at boot: `BuildEvent` in `provider/internal/provider/buildEvent.go` is invoked by kairos-init during the build, and it runs the k0s installer script, relocates the binary from `/usr/local/bin/k0s` to `/usr/bin/k0s`, and writes the service units by hand. None of that is exercised until release day.

This is not hypothetical. #4299 (k0s control-plane components fall back to root because the native system users are not created) is exactly a build-time defect on that path, and it reached a release unnoticed. When approving the fix (#4469) the reviewer asked for this gap to be filed separately, which is what this issue is.

### 2. The tag scheme silently collides, which is why a k0s cell cannot just be added

`reusable-factory.yaml` computes the `$K8S` tag segment gated on the **version**:

```bash
K8S=""
if [[ -n "$KUBERNETES_VERSION" ]]; then
  K8S="-$KUBERNETES_DISTRO-$SANITIZED_KUBERNETES_VERSION"
fi
```

`kubernetes_version` defaults to `auto`, and `auto` resolves to the empty string a few lines earlier so kairos-init can pick the version itself. `pr.yaml` and `master.yaml` both take that default. So on those two paths `$K8S` is **always empty**, and the distro never reaches the tag.

The default `custom_tag_format` is `$FLAVOR-$FLAVOR_RELEASE-$VARIANT-$ARCH-$MODEL$K8S-$VERSION$UKI`, and `VARIANT` is derived as `standard` for both k3s and k0s. So an `amd64-standard-k0s` cell added today would push to the same tag as the existing `amd64-standard` (k3s) cell:

```
ghcr.io/kairos-io/kairos/hadron:hadron-v0.5.1-standard-amd64-generic-<version>
```

Both cells run in the same matrix with `fail-fast: false`, so whichever finishes last wins. `test-standard` and `test-standard-encryption` then pull that tag by reconstructing it (`reusable-qemu-test.yaml`, "Set Image tag"), which means sixteen qemu cells could boot a k0s image while reporting as k3s coverage. No error, no warning.

Same failure class as #4310, and same class as the artifact-name collision that already bit `v4.3.0-rc3` (documented in the `custom_artifact_format` comment in `_build-iso.yaml`).

### The inconsistency that shows which side is wrong

Fifty lines below the `$K8S` block, in the same step, the default artifact name gates on the **distro**:

```bash
if [[ -n "$KUBERNETES_DISTRO" ]]; then
  DEFAULT_ARTIFACT_NAME="$DEFAULT_ARTIFACT_NAME-$KUBERNETES_DISTRO-$SANITIZED_KUBERNETES_VERSION"
fi
```

That is the correct condition: the distro is known whether or not the version was pinned, and it is the distro that distinguishes two otherwise identical cells. The `$K8S` block and `DEFAULT_TAG` should use the same test. (The artifact block has a cosmetic bug of its own: with `auto` it appends a bare trailing `-`.)

`release.yaml` is unaffected either way, because all of its k8s cells pin `kubernetes_version` explicitly, so `$K8S` is already non-empty there.

## Suggested fix

1. Derive `$K8S` (and `DEFAULT_TAG`, and the artifact name) from `KUBERNETES_DISTRO`, appending the sanitized version only when it is non-empty.
2. Keep the two hand-written mirrors of that tag in lockstep: `reusable-qemu-test.yaml` and `_uki-test.yaml` both reconstruct the tag in shell, and both currently hardcode `K8S=""`. They need to derive it the same way, which also means `pr.yaml`/`master.yaml` must pass `kubernetes_distro` to the test jobs (`test-standard` and the UKI cells run against `k3s` images but do not currently say so).
3. Then add a k0s cell. It does not need to be a full ISO: `iso: false` builds and pushes the OS container image only, which is where `BuildEvent` runs, so the #4299 class of bug is caught for the cost of one image build rather than an ISO plus a qemu boot.

Runtime k0s coverage (does the cluster actually come up) stays a separate, larger gap; this issue is only about catching build-time regressions before a tag is cut.
title: CI: no job builds a k0s image, and the tag scheme drops the k8s distro when the version is 'auto' so one cannot be added

author: tbrasser
body:
## Summary

The Hadron composer in the Artifact Builder generates images that boot without firmware on real hardware, because it relocates firmware onto a path that Kairos mounts over at runtime. The same generated RUN block also breaks Hadron's merged-/usr layout.

Both defects are in the generated middle section (`ui/src/pages/ArtifactBuilder.tsx`, `renderHadronMiddleContent`):

## Defect 1: firmware ends up where COS_PERSISTENT hides it

On an installed Kairos node, persistent state is mounted over `/usr/local`.
The composer moves firmware to `/usr/local/lib/firmware` and points `/lib/firmware` at it — so after the first boot from disk, the firmware baked into the image is shadowed by the persistent mount and the kernel finds nothing.

Observed consequence on bare metal (Ryzen AI Max+ 395 / gfx1151, Realtek 8127 10GbE, MediaTek MT7925): the machine comes up with no NIC and no GPU firmware — unrecoverable without console access, and invisible at build time because the image itself is fine.

Firmware must stay under `/usr/lib/firmware` (the upstream hadron-firmware layer images already ship blobs at their native paths; the relocation RUN is what moves them). If the relocation exists to support some layering scheme, that scheme needs a runtime home that is not shadowed by `/usr/local` — but simply not relocating works and matches what the base Hadron image expects.

## Defect 2: merged-/usr is broken for /usr/sbin

Hadron is a from-scratch merged-/usr system where `/usr/sbin` is a symlink to `bin`. The composer deletes that symlink and creates a real directory. Anything that lived "in sbin" via the symlink — e.g. PAM's `unix_chkpwd`, which pam_unix looks up by absolute path — becomes unreachable, and the live-mode root autologin degrades to a blinking-cursor loop. (We hit exactly this class when a layer (I believe GPG) shipped a real `usr/sbin/`, which is why our image verification now asserts `readlink /usr/sbin == bin`.)

If the goal is to let layers add sbin content, the safe direction on a merged-/usr base is the opposite: leave the symlink alone and let COPY follow it into `/usr/bin`, or normalize layer contents like the base does.

## Suggested fix

Drop the relocation entirely: no `/usr/local/lib/firmware`, no `/lib/firmware` rewrite, no `/usr/sbin` replacement. Firmware and layer payloads then land at their native merged-/usr paths and survive the persistent mount.

## Environment / evidence

- AuroraBoot main as of 2026-08 (still present; also in v0.26.x)
- Hadron v0.4.x base, Kairos v4, installed (not live-mode) nodes
- Our image pipeline asserts firmware presence under /usr/lib/firmware and the merged-/usr symlink, which is how both defects were caught before flashing

Happy to test a fixed composer end-to-end on a three-node bare-metal fleet (Realtek/Aquantia NICs, amdgpu gfx1151, MT7925 Wi-Fi) and report boot, firmware-load and runtime results.
title: Auroraboot Hadron composer: generated image hides firmware behind the runtime /usr/local mount (and breaks merged-/usr)

author: JustWilder
body:
**Kairos version:**

Current image:

```text
hadron:v0.2.0-standard-amd64-generic-v4.1.0-k3s-v1.36.0-k3s1
```

Output from `cat /etc/os-release`:

```text
NAME="Hadron Linux"
PRETTY_NAME="Hadron Linux"
ID=hadron
BUILD_ID=rolling
VERSION_ID="v0.2.0"
```

Output from `cat /etc/kairos-release`:

```text
KAIROS_ARCH="amd64"
KAIROS_BUG_REPORT_URL="https://github.com/kairos-io/kairos/issues"
KAIROS_FAMILY="hadron"
KAIROS_FIPS="false"
KAIROS_FLAVOR="hadron"
KAIROS_FLAVOR_RELEASE="v0.2.0"
KAIROS_HOME_URL="https://github.com/kairos-io/kairos"
KAIROS_ID="kairos"
KAIROS_ID_LIKE="kairos-standard-hadron-v0.2.0"
KAIROS_INIT_VERSION="v0.13.0"
KAIROS_MODEL="generic"
KAIROS_NAME="kairos-standard-hadron-v0.2.0"
KAIROS_RELEASE="v4.1.0"
KAIROS_SOFTWARE_VERSION="v1.36.0+k3s1"
KAIROS_SOFTWARE_VERSION_PREFIX="k3s"
KAIROS_TARGETARCH="amd64"
KAIROS_TRUSTED_BOOT="false"
KAIROS_VARIANT="standard"
KAIROS_VERSION="v4.1.0"
```

**CPU architecture, OS, and Version:**

```text
standard-amd64-generic
```

Output from `uname -a`:

```text
Linux helios-1 7.0.6-hadron #1 SMP PREEMPT_DYNAMIC Tue May 12 16:17:04 UTC 2026 x86_64 GNU/Linux
```

**Describe the bug**

After upgrading from Kairos Ubuntu-based images to Hadron, SSH stopped working on all nodes. The nodes were still online and Kubernetes reported them as Ready, but SSH to port 22 failed with:

```text
ssh: connect to host <node-ip> port 22: Connection refused
```

The root cause appears to be a stale systemd symlink persisted from the previous Ubuntu-based image:

```text
/etc/systemd/system/sshd.service -> /usr/lib/systemd/system/ssh.service
```

On the Hadron image, the valid packaged unit is:

```text
/usr/lib/systemd/system/sshd.service
```

But this target does not exist:

```text
/usr/lib/systemd/system/ssh.service
```

Because `/etc/systemd/system/sshd.service` shadows the packaged Hadron unit, systemd resolves `sshd.service` through the stale symlink and marks the service as bad/not found.

The cloud-configs define the `kairos` user and SSH authorized keys, so this does not appear to be a missing user/key configuration issue [1][2][3][4].

**To Reproduce**

Upgrade a cluster through this image path:

```text
ubuntu:24.10-standard-amd64-generic-v3.4.2-k3s-v1.32.3-k3s1
ubuntu:25.10-standard-amd64-generic-v3.7.2-k3s-v1.33.7-k3s3
ubuntu:25.10-standard-amd64-generic-v3.7.2-k3s-v1.34.3-k3s3
hadron:v0.2.0-standard-amd64-generic-v4.1.0-k3s-v1.35.4-k3s1
hadron:v0.2.0-standard-amd64-generic-v4.1.0-k3s-v1.36.0-k3s1
```

Cluster layout:

```text
helios-1   10.10.101.1   control-plane
helios-2   10.10.101.2   control-plane
helios-3   10.10.101.3   control-plane
vulcan-1   10.10.101.4   worker
```

Those static node IPs are configured in the node cloud-configs [1][2][3][4].

After upgrade, SSH failed on all nodes:

```bash
ssh kairos@10.10.101.1
ssh kairos@10.10.101.2
ssh kairos@10.10.101.3
ssh kairos@10.10.101.4
```

**Expected behavior**

SSH should remain available after upgrade for the configured `kairos` user and authorized SSH keys.

**Logs**

Systemd showed:

```text
sshd.service bad enabled
```

And:

```text
LoadState=not-found
FragmentPath=
SourcePath=
UnitFileState=
LoadError=org.freedesktop.systemd1.NoSuchUnit "Unit sshd.service not found."
```

The stale symlink was present:

```text
/etc/systemd/system/sshd.service -> /usr/lib/systemd/system/ssh.service
```

The valid Hadron unit existed:

```text
/usr/lib/systemd/system/sshd.service
```

The packaged Hadron unit was:

```ini
[Unit]
Description=OpenSSH Daemon
After=network.target sshkeygen.service
Before=ssh-access.target
Wants=sshkeygen.service ssh-access.target

[Service]
Type=notify-reload
ExecStart=/usr/bin/sshd -D
KillMode=process
Restart=always

[Install]
WantedBy=multi-user.target
```

Manual start of `sshd` worked:

```bash
mkdir -p /run/sshd
/usr/sbin/sshd -t -f /etc/ssh/sshd_config
/usr/sbin/sshd -E /tmp/sshd.log -f /etc/ssh/sshd_config
```

Output:

```text
Server listening on 0.0.0.0 port 22.
Server listening on :: port 22.
```

After that, SSH login worked.

**Workaround**

Remove the stale symlink and enable the packaged Hadron unit:

```bash
sudo rm -f /etc/systemd/system/sshd.service
sudo systemctl daemon-reload
sudo systemctl reset-failed sshd.service
sudo systemctl enable --now sshd.service
```

Expected fixed state:

```bash
systemctl show sshd.service -p LoadState -p FragmentPath -p UnitFileState
```

```text
LoadState=loaded
FragmentPath=/usr/lib/systemd/system/sshd.service
UnitFileState=enabled
```

If `sshd` was manually started first for recovery, `systemctl start sshd.service` may fail with:

```text
Bind to port 22 on 0.0.0.0 failed: Address in use
Bind to port 22 on :: failed: Address in use
fatal: Cannot bind any address
```

In that case, stop only the manually-started listener and then start the systemd service.

**Additional context**

This looks like an upgrade artifact from the Ubuntu-based Kairos image line to Hadron. The stale symlink points to an Ubuntu-style service name:

```text
/usr/lib/systemd/system/ssh.service
```

But Hadron provides:

```text
/usr/lib/systemd/system/sshd.service
```

The issue affected all four upgraded nodes. Kubernetes stayed functional, but direct SSH access was lost until the stale symlink was removed.

Potential fixes could be:

1. remove stale `/etc/systemd/system/sshd.service` symlinks pointing to missing `/usr/lib/systemd/system/ssh.service`,
2. ship a compatibility alias for `ssh.service`,
3. or document this as a required migration cleanup step when moving from Ubuntu-based Kairos images to Hadron.

Note: cloud-configs contain K3s configuration and any `K3S_TOKEN` values have been redacted before posting.
title: SSH fails after upgrade from Kairos Ubuntu image to Hadron due to stale /etc/systemd/system/sshd.service symlink
